docs.text: Design guides cover design decisions, platform behavior, and architectural considerations for working with Business Events. Unlike scenarios, which walk through a complete solution end to end, design guides focus on a single concept you can apply across any project.

docs.title: Event-Driven Architectures in Microsoft Fabric
docs.text:
In a traditional data platform, workloads communicate by polling or direct calls: a service checks for changes on a schedule, or one workload calls another and waits for a response. This works, but it creates fragile dependencies and wastes compute on work that may find nothing to process.

Event-driven architecture inverts this model. Instead of asking "has something changed?", workloads signal "something happened" the moment it occurs. Any interested service reacts immediately, independently, and only when there is real work to do.

docs.title: Why it matters for Fabric
docs.text:
Microsoft Fabric is a unified platform where notebooks, pipelines, eventstreams, and analytics workloads run side by side. This creates natural opportunities for event-driven patterns: a notebook that finishes a transformation can signal downstream consumers, a threshold condition in a stream can trigger an alert, a pipeline completion can kick off the next stage automatically.

Without an event model, these interactions require scheduled triggers, hard-coded dependencies, or manual orchestration. With events, each workload stays focused on its own responsibility and reacts to what matters.

docs.title: The three event pillars
docs.text:
Business Events are explicitly defined and published by your code. You decide what the event represents, what data it carries, and when it fires.

docs.title: Handling Retries
docs.text:
Business Events includes built-in retry behavior. If delivery does not succeed on the first attempt, the platform automatically retries for up to 24 hours. After that window, the event is no longer retried.

This means retry handling is fully managed — you do not need to implement retry logic in your publisher or consumer.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    P[Publisher] -->|Publishes event| BE[Business Event\n'Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold']
    BE -->|Delivery attempt| C[Consumer]
    C -->|Delivery fails| BE
    BE -->|Retries automatically\nfor up to 24 hours| C
    BE -->|After 24 hours\nno more retries| X[Event expired]

docs.title: What this means for publishers
docs.text:
Your publish call succeeds as soon as the platform accepts the event. You do not need to:

  • Implement exponential backoff
  • Track delivery status
  • Re-publish on failure
# This is all you need — no retry wrapper required
notebookutils.businessEvents.publish(
    workspace, schema_set, event_type, event_data, dataVersion='v1'
)

docs.title: What this means for consumers
docs.text: Consumers should be idempotent — designed to handle receiving the same event more than once without side effects. Because the platform retries on delivery failure, a consumer that partially processed an event and then failed may receive it again.

docs.title: Making consumers idempotent
docs.text:
Use the CloudEvents id field (available in the envelope) as a deduplication key:

// In Eventhouse — check if event was already processed
['Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold']
| where id == "a8f3c1d2-..."
| count

For Activator, idempotency is handled naturally — the alert condition evaluates each event independently.

docs.title: Retry window considerations
docs.text: Scenario Recommendation Event represents a time-sensitive signal (e.g., fraud alert) Design consumers to process quickly; stale delivery within 24h may still be actionable Event drives a one-time action (e.g., send email) Make the action idempotent or check for duplicates before acting Consumer is temporarily unavailable Events will be retried — no publisher changes needed

docs.title: Multi-Consumer Fanout
docs.text: Fanout is a pattern where a single Business Event is consumed by multiple independent consumers simultaneously. Because Business Events is a pub/sub system, publishers do not need to know how many consumers exist — each consumer subscribes independently.

docs.title: One event, many consumers
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    P[Publisher
Notebook / UDF / Eventstream] -->|publish| BE[Business Event
'Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert']
    BE -->|consume| A[Activator
Send Teams alert]
    BE -->|consume| B[Eventhouse
Store for analytics]
    BE -->|consume| C[Activator
Trigger reorder pipeline]

Each consumer subscribes independently. Adding a new consumer does not require any change to the publisher.

docs.title: Alert + analytics
docs.text:
The most common combination — one consumer reacts in real time, another stores for historical analysis.

flowchart LR
    P[Publisher] -->|publish| BE[Business Event\n'Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert']
    BE -->|consume| ACT[Activator\nReal-time alert]
    BE -->|consume| EH[Eventhouse\nHistorical analytics]

When to use: Any event where you need both immediate action and long-term visibility.

docs.title: Alert + automation
docs.text:
Two Activator consumers with different actions — one notifies a human, another triggers an automated workflow.

flowchart LR
    P[Publisher] -->|publish| BE[Business Event\n'Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert']
    BE -->|consume| A1[Activator Rule 1\nSend email notification]
    BE -->|consume| A2[Activator Rule 2\nTrigger Power Automate flow]

When to use: When a signal requires both human awareness and an automated response, and you want to manage them independently.

docs.title: Cross-domain fanout
docs.text:
A single business signal consumed by teams in different domains, each with their own logic.

flowchart LR
    P[Publisher
Retail workload] -->|publish| BE[Business Event
'Retail.Customer.MilestoneReached']
    BE -->|consume| A[Marketing team
Activator → loyalty email]
    BE -->|consume| B[Analytics team
Eventhouse → cohort analysis]
    BE -->|consume| C[Finance team
Activator → discount approval]

When to use: When a business signal has value across multiple teams or domains, and each team should own their consumer independently.

docs.title: How to set up fanout
docs.text:
Each consumer is created independently — there is no fanout configuration on the publisher side.

Consumer How to add Activator Real-Time Hub → Business events → Set alert → configure new rule Eventhouse Enabled at Business Event creation time via the "Analyze in Eventhouse" checkbox

To add a second Activator consumer, simply create a new alert rule on the same Business Event. The two rules run independently and do not interfere with each other.

docs.title: Design considerations
docs.text:
Keep consumers independent. Each consumer should be able to fail, restart, or be updated without affecting others.

Do not use fanout to sequence work. If Consumer B must run after Consumer A completes, fanout is not the right pattern — use a dedicated orchestration mechanism instead.

Monitor each consumer separately. A delivery failure to one consumer does not affect delivery to others. Track consumer health individually.

docs.title: Schema Versioning
docs.text: Business Event schemas can evolve over time. This pattern covers how to update a schema and what changes are required on both the publisher and consumer side.

docs.title: Where schemas live
docs.text:
Schemas are stored as Event Schemas inside an Event Schema Set in the Event Schema Registry. When you create a Business Event from Real-Time Hub, a schema is created automatically in the associated schema set.

To evolve a schema:

  1. Go to the Event Schema Set in the Event Schema Registry
  2. Open the schema you want to update
  3. Add, modify, or remove fields
  4. Save the new version — the platform increments the version number automatically

docs.title: What changes after a schema update
docs.text:
A schema update does not propagate automatically to publishers or consumers. Both sides must be updated explicitly.

flowchart TD
    A[Update schema in
Event Schema Registry] --> B[Update publisher
to send new version]
    A --> C[Create new consumer
subscription for new version]
    B --> D[Publisher sends
dataVersion v2]
    C --> E[Consumer receives
v2 events]

docs.title: Publisher update
docs.text:
The publisher must send the new dataVersion and include any new or changed fields in the payload:

# Before — v1
event_data = {
    "store_id": "STR-001",
    "product_id": "SKU-9821",
    "current_qty": 4
}
notebookutils.businessEvents.publish(
    workspace, schema_set, event_type, event_data, dataVersion="v1"
)

# After — v2 adds threshold_pct field
event_data = {
    "store_id": "STR-001",
    "product_id": "SKU-9821",
    "current_qty": 4,
    "threshold_pct": 0.15       # new field in v2
}
notebookutils.businessEvents.publish(
    workspace, schema_set, event_type, event_data, dataVersion="v2"
)

docs.title: Consumer update
docs.text:
Each consumer subscription is tied to a specific schema version. To consume the new version:

  • Activator — create a new alert rule targeting the updated Business Event
  • Eventhouse — a new KQL table is created for the new version; update your queries to reference it

Existing subscriptions keep receiving the old version

Subscriptions created for v1 continue to receive v1 events. They do not automatically upgrade to v2. You must create new subscriptions and migrate consumers deliberately.

docs.title: Versioning strategy
docs.text: Approach When to use Additive change (add new optional fields) Safe — existing consumers ignore unknown fields Breaking change (rename or remove fields) Requires new version and explicit consumer migration Parallel versions (run v1 and v2 simultaneously) Use during migration; decommission v1 once all consumers are updated

docs.title: Recommendations
docs.text:
Start with v1 from day one. Always publish with an explicit dataVersion so you have room to evolve without disruption.

Prefer additive changes. Adding new optional fields to a schema is the least disruptive path — consumers that do not need the new fields continue working without changes.

Communicate version changes to consumers. Because subscriptions do not auto-upgrade, consumer teams need to know when a new version is available so they can create updated subscriptions.

docs.title: Structuring Payloads
docs.text: A Business Event is more than a data record — it is a signal that something meaningful happened in your business. Designing a good payload means capturing enough context for any consumer to act on the event without needing to query additional systems.

docs.title: What makes a good business signal
docs.text:
A well-structured Business Event answers three questions:

Question Example field What happened? event_type: "Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert" What was involved? store_id, product_id, threshold_qty When and where? occurred_at, region

Keep payloads factual and immutable — describe what happened, not what should happen next. Decisions belong to the consumer, not the event.

docs.title: Anatomy of a Business Event schema
docs.text:
When you create a Business Event in Real-Time Hub, you define a schema with typed fields. These fields become the payload that publishers send and consumers receive.

{
  "store_id": "STR-001",
  "product_id": "SKU-9821",
  "current_qty": 4,
  "threshold_qty": 10,
  "occurred_at": "2024-11-15T14:32:00Z"
}

docs.title: Field type reference
docs.text: Type Use for string IDs, names, categories, status values int Counts, quantities, ranks float Prices, percentages, measurements boolean Flags, toggles

docs.title: CloudEvents under the hood
docs.text:
Business Events uses the CloudEvents specification as its envelope format. When you publish a payload, the platform wraps it automatically with standard metadata:

{
  "specversion": "1.0",
  "type": "Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold",
  "source": "/tenants/{tenant-id}/workspaces/{workspace-id}/items/{item-id}",
  "id": "a8f3c1d2-...",
  "time": "2024-11-15T14:32:00Z",
  "dataversion": "v1",
  "data": {
    "store_id": "STR-001",
    "product_id": "SKU-9821",
    "current_qty": 4,
    "threshold_qty": 10,
    "occurred_at": "2024-11-15T14:32:00Z"
  }
}

You only define and send the data block. The CloudEvents envelope (specversion, source, id, time) is added by the platform.

docs.title: What this means for consumers
docs.text:
• Activator receives the full CloudEvents envelope and lets you reference fields inside data directly in your alert conditions
  • Eventhouse stores the data fields as columns in the KQL table, with the envelope metadata available as additional columns

docs.title: Design guidelines
docs.text:
Include a timestamp in your payload. Even though the envelope has a time field, having occurred_at inside data lets you capture the business moment precisely — for example, when a transaction was processed, not when the event was published.

Use stable, opaque IDs. Field values like store_id or run_id should be identifiers that consumers can use to look up additional context if needed. Avoid embedding mutable state.

Keep payloads flat when possible. Nested objects are supported but make KQL queries and Activator field mapping more complex. Prefer flat structures unless nesting is semantically meaningful.

Version from the start. Always publish with dataVersion="v1". When the schema evolves, increment the version rather than changing existing fields. See Schema Versioning for details.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text: Business Events connect existing detection workloads with independent consumers through a shared event contract in Microsoft Fabric. A notebook, function, stream, or rule can keep recognizing a business condition while publishing a representation that other teams can reuse. This page explains how the components fit together.

docs.title: High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph Publishers["Detect in existing workloads"]
        NB[Notebook]
        UDF[User Data Function]
        ES[Eventstream]
        ACT_P[Activator]
    end

    BE1(["Business Event<br/>Sales volume alert"])
    BE2(["Business Event<br/>Low stock threshold"])
    BE3(["Business Event<br/>Pipeline run completed"])

    ACT_C["Activator<br/>Rules and actions"]
    EH[("Eventhouse<br/>KQL analysis")]

    NB -->|publish| BE1
    UDF -->|publish| BE2
    ES -->|publish| BE3
    ACT_P -->|publish| BE1

    BE1 -->|consume| ACT_C
    BE2 -->|consume| ACT_C
    BE1 -->|consume| EH
    BE3 -->|consume| EH

Read from top to bottom: existing detection workloads, shared Business Event contracts, then independent consumers. Arrows show publication and consumption, not a required processing sequence across consumers. These are example routes, not an exhaustive compatibility matrix. Short event labels map to the full names below.

Diagram label Event type Sales volume alert Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert Low stock threshold Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold Pipeline run completed DataOps.Pipeline.RunCompleted

Real-Time Hub is the entry point for creating and discovering Business Events. The Event Schema Registry is a platform-level capability, not a runtime stage between the publisher and consumer.

docs.title: Event Schema Registry
docs.text:
The Event Schema Registry is a platform-level capability in Microsoft Fabric that stores and validates all schema definitions. Business Events are a special type of event schema stored in the registry, organized into Event Schema Sets.

flowchart TB
    subgraph Definition["Definition and organization, not runtime flow"]
        ESR["Event Schema Registry<br/>Platform capability"]
        SS["Event Schema Set<br/>Groups schemas"]
        BE(["Business Event schema<br/>Sales volume alert"])
        ESR ---|organizes| SS
        SS ---|contains| BE
    end

Lines show schema organization, not event delivery. The example schema is Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert; the runtime publication and consumption paths are shown in the high-level architecture above.

Business Events cannot be created directly from the Event Schema Registry. They must be created from Real-Time Hub → Business Events. During creation, you can create a new Event Schema Set inline or select an existing one. The Event Schema Registry is the underlying storage; Real-Time Hub → Business Events is the entry point.

Before publishing, go to Real-Time Hub → Business Events and create your Business Event from there. You will be prompted to create or select an Event Schema Set as part of the flow.

docs.title: Publishers
docs.text:
Any workload that detects a meaningful condition and signals it to the rest of the platform.

Publisher Best suited for Notebook Batch analysis results, data quality checks, scheduled monitoring User Data Function External webhook normalization, custom integrations Eventstream Real-time stream threshold conditions Activator Re-publishing derived events from existing rules

docs.title: Real-Time Hub
docs.text: The entry point for creating and discovering Business Events in Microsoft Fabric. Event schemas are organized in Event Schema Sets in the platform-level Event Schema Registry; the diagram does not imply that the registry is hosted inside the Real-Time Hub interface.

docs.title: Consumers
docs.text:
Workloads that subscribe to one or more Business Events and react when a matching event arrives.

Consumer Best suited for Activator Triggering alerts, notifications, or downstream actions based on event conditions Eventhouse Persisting events for historical analysis and KQL queries

docs.title: One event, multiple consumers
docs.text:
A single Business Event can support independent responses in multiple consumers. Adding a consumer that uses the existing contract does not require changing the publisher.

flowchart LR
    NB[Notebook] -->|publish| BE(["Business Event<br/>Sales volume alert"])
    BE -->|consume| ACT["Activator<br/>Send Teams alert"]
    BE -->|consume| EH[("Eventhouse<br/>Log for audit")]

The event is Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert. Both consumers use the same contract; neither waits for the other to complete.

This fan-out pattern separates detection from downstream responses. It is useful when several teams need the same finding, while direct service calls remain appropriate when a workload needs an immediate response to continue.

docs.title: Decision Guide
docs.text: Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence offers multiple ways to detect conditions, move data, and trigger responses. Start with what your existing implementation already does, then decide whether you also need a shared event contract. These capabilities can work together rather than replace one another.

docs.title: Capabilities at a glance
docs.text: Capability What it is Best for Business Events Schema-defined signals published by Fabric workloads to Real-Time Hub Discrete, meaningful occurrences that need to reach one or more consumers independently Eventstream High-throughput streaming pipeline for continuous data IoT telemetry, clickstreams, logs, and any high-volume continuous data Activator Rules engine that monitors data and triggers actions Reacting to conditions in streams or Business Events without writing code Direct API call HTTP call made from a Notebook or User Data Function to an external service When you need a synchronous response from a service outside Fabric

docs.title: Should I use Business Events?
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[I need to signal that\nsomething happened] --> B{Is it a continuous\nstream of data?}
    B -->|Yes: high-volume, ongoing| Z1[Use Eventstream]
    B -->|No: a discrete condition occurred| C{Do other workloads\nneed to act on this?}
    C -->|Yes| E[Use Business Events ✅]
    C -->|No: I need an immediate\nresponse to continue| Z2[Make a direct API call\nfrom a Notebook or UDF]

docs.title: When to use each option in Fabric
docs.text:
Use Business Events when:

  • A Notebook finishes a transformation and Activator or Eventhouse need to react
  • A threshold condition is detected and multiple consumers need to be notified independently
  • You want to add a new consumer without modifying the publisher
  • Multiple teams need a common representation of the same detected business condition
  • You need an explicit schema contract for the data the event carries

Use Eventstream when:

  • You are ingesting continuous data from IoT sensors, event producers, or external systems
  • You need to process or route high-volume data streams in real time
  • You need to process raw records before deciding which business conditions matter

Eventstream can also publish a Business Event when its processing detects a meaningful condition. The stream carries the underlying records; the Business Event represents the finding that other teams need.

Use Activator directly when:

  • You want to monitor an existing Eventstream or Eventhouse table for conditions
  • You need to trigger alerts or actions without publishing an explicit event
  • The logic lives entirely within Activator and no other consumer needs the signal

Make a direct API call when:

  • You are in a Notebook or User Data Function and need a synchronous response from an external service
  • The call is to a system outside Fabric (a REST API, a database, an external platform)
  • You need the result immediately to continue execution in the same workload

docs.title: Event Schema
docs.text: Every Business Event in Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Hub is defined by a schema before any data is published. The schema describes the structure and types of the event payload.

docs.title: What you define vs. what Real-Time Hub handles
docs.text:
Business Events are built on CloudEvents 1.0, an industry-standard specification for describing event data. However, you do not need to interact with the CloudEvents envelope directly. Real-Time Hub handles the transport layer for you.

Your responsibility is to define only the business properties of the event: what data it carries and what each field means.

Layer Managed by Example Transport envelope Real-Time Hub CloudEvents headers, routing, delivery Business payload You store_id, deviation_pct, severity

docs.title: Schema format
docs.text:
Business Events use a record schema with the following top-level structure:

{
  "type": "record",
  "name": "<EventName>",
  "fields": [
    {
      "name": "<field_name>",
      "type": "<field_type>",
      "doc": "<description>"
    }
  ]
}
Property Required Description type Yes Always "record" name Yes PascalCase name identifying the event type fields Yes Array of field definitions

docs.title: Field definition
docs.text:
Each field in the fields array has the following properties:

Property Required Description name Yes Field name (snake_case recommended) type Yes Data type of the field doc No Human-readable description of the field

docs.title: Supported field types
docs.text: Type Description Example value string UTF-8 text "store-mx-042" int 32-bit integer 1250 float 32-bit floating point -40.6 boolean True or false true

docs.title: Example schema
docs.text:
The following schema defines a Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert event with six fields. This JSON represents the schema you define when creating a Business Event in Real-Time Hub → Business Events. During creation, you can paste this directly into the code editor. If you need a new Event Schema Set, you can create one inline as part of the Business Event creation flow, or select an existing one.

{
  "type": "record",
  "name": "Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert",
  "fields": [
    {
      "name": "store_id",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "Unique identifier of the store reporting the alert"
    },
    {
      "name": "expected_transactions",
      "type": "int",
      "doc": "Expected number of transactions based on historical average"
    },
    {
      "name": "actual_transactions",
      "type": "int",
      "doc": "Actual transactions recorded in the current monitoring window"
    },
    {
      "name": "deviation_pct",
      "type": "float",
      "doc": "Percentage deviation from expected volume. Negative means below expected."
    },
    {
      "name": "window_start",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "Start of the monitoring window in ISO 8601 format"
    },
    {
      "name": "severity",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "Alert severity level: low, medium, high"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Schema naming conventions
docs.text: Convention Example name (event) PascalCase: VolumeAlert, LowStockThreshold name (field) snake_case: store_id, deviation_pct doc (field) Complete sentence describing the field's purpose and expected values

docs.title: Namespaces (optional but recommended)
docs.text:
For projects with multiple event types across different business domains, prefixing the event name with a namespace prevents naming collisions and makes the event's origin immediately clear.

The recommended pattern is Domain.Subdomain.EventName in PascalCase:

Without namespace With namespace VolumeAlert Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert LowStockThreshold Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold RunCompleted DataOps.Pipeline.RunCompleted

All examples in this repository follow the namespace convention.

docs.title: What are Business Events?
docs.text:
A Business Event is a named, schema-defined representation of a meaningful business occurrence or detected condition. It gives teams a shared contract for communicating situations such as inventory falling below a threshold, a shipment being delayed, or a customer reaching a loyalty milestone.

The business signal is the meaning of that situation. The Business Event is how you represent and share an occurrence of it. Your existing notebooks, queries, rules, and applications can continue detecting the signal; consumers use the published event to support decisions, automation, and analysis.

Official documentation

For the complete API reference and platform overview, see the Business Events documentation on learn.microsoft.com.

docs.title: The core idea
docs.text:
Your team may already detect important conditions and respond through dashboards, alerts, or application integrations. The challenge grows when other teams need the same signal: each implementation may use a different name, interpretation, or payload, and a change to the business definition requires coordination across them.

Business Events provide a reusable representation of that signal. A publisher (a Notebook, a User Data Function, an Eventstream, or Activator) publishes an occurrence through Real-Time Hub. Consumers, such as Activator and Eventhouse, use that event independently, without the publisher calling each one.

For example, the same low-stock event can support an operations alert and inventory analysis. Adding a consumer that uses the existing contract does not require changing the publisher. Teams still need to agree on the signal's meaning, ownership, and evolution; the schema alone does not establish that agreement.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Publishers
        NB[Notebook]
        UDF[User Data Function]
        ES[Eventstream]
        ACT1[Activator]
    end

    subgraph RTH[Real-Time Hub]
        BE([Business Event\n'Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert'])
    end

    subgraph Consumers
        ACT2[Activator]
        EH[Eventhouse]
    end

    NB -->|publish| BE
    UDF -->|publish| BE
    ES -->|publish| BE
    ACT1 -->|publish| BE
    BE -->|consume| ACT2
    BE -->|consume| EH

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
Schema-first design Every Business Event has a defined schema before publication. The schema uses a record format with typed fields, giving publishers and consumers an explicit data contract. Document what those fields mean and coordinate changes to that contract.

Decoupled architecture Publishers do not call each consumer directly. Consumers depend on the event contract rather than a direct call from a particular publisher. New consumers can reuse that contract without changes to the publishing code.

Real-time delivery Events reach configured consumers through Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Hub infrastructure. Detection frequency and downstream processing also affect how quickly the business can respond.

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text: Recipes are short, focused code snippets that solve one specific task. They are smaller than a full scenario — no business context, no architecture diagram — just the code you need.

docs.title: Available recipes
docs.text: Recipe Description Chain Two Business Events Use the output of one event as the trigger for another Batch Publish from a Notebook Publish multiple events in a single Notebook run Batch Publish from a User Data Function Publish multiple events from a UDF using an array payload

docs.title: Batch Publish from a Notebook
docs.text: Publish multiple Business Events in a single Notebook call — useful for processing a list of records and signaling each one as an individual business event.

docs.title: When to use this recipe
docs.text: Use batch publishing when your Notebook processes a collection of items and each item should generate its own event. For example, after a daily inventory check, publish one Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold event per product that is below threshold.

docs.title: Batch publish with an array payload
docs.text:
Pass a list of dictionaries as event_data to publish multiple events in a single call:

from datetime import datetime, timezone

low_stock_items = [
    {"product_id": "SKU-9821", "store_id": "STR-001", "current_qty": 4, "threshold_qty": 10},
    {"product_id": "SKU-4432", "store_id": "STR-003", "current_qty": 2, "threshold_qty": 15},
    {"product_id": "SKU-7751", "store_id": "STR-007", "current_qty": 1, "threshold_qty": 5},
]

event_data = [
    {**item, "occurred_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()}
    for item in low_stock_items
]

notebookutils.businessEvents.publish(
    "MyWorkspace",
    "RetailInventory",
    "Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold",
    event_data,
    dataVersion="v1"
)

docs.title: Considerations
docs.text:
Publish only what changed. Filter your dataset before building the array — include only items that crossed a threshold, not every item in the inventory.

Each item in the array becomes an independent event. The platform delivers each one individually, with its own retry window.

Avoid very large arrays. If you need to publish thousands of events per second, consider using Eventstream with a streaming source instead of a Notebook call.

docs.title: Batch Publish from a User Data Function
docs.text: Publish multiple Business Events in a single User Data Function call by passing an array as the event data.

docs.title: When to use this recipe
docs.text: Use batch publishing from a UDF when your function processes a collection of items and each item should generate its own event — for example, when multiple inventory updates arrive together and each one should produce an independent event.

docs.title: Batch publish with an array payload
docs.text:
The key difference from a single-event publish is that event_data is a list of dictionaries instead of a single dictionary:

import fabric.functions as fn
import json
from datetime import datetime, timezone

udf = fn.UserDataFunctions()

@udf.connection(argName="businessEventsClient", alias="RetailInventory")
@udf.function()
def batch_publish(
    businessEventsClient: fn.FabricBusinessEventsClient,
    items_json: str
) -> str:
    items = json.loads(items_json)

    event_data = [
        {
            "store_id": item["store_id"],
            "product_id": item["product_id"],
            "current_qty": item["current_qty"],
            "threshold_qty": item["threshold_qty"],
            "occurred_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()
        }
        for item in items
    ]

    businessEventsClient.PublishEvent(
        type="Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold",
        event_data=event_data,
        data_version="v1"
    )

    return f"Published {len(event_data)} events"

docs.title: Example input
docs.text:
Pass a JSON string as the items_json parameter when calling the function:

[
  { "store_id": "STR-001", "product_id": "SKU-9821", "current_qty": 4, "threshold_qty": 10 },
  { "store_id": "STR-003", "product_id": "SKU-4432", "current_qty": 2, "threshold_qty": 15 },
  { "store_id": "STR-007", "product_id": "SKU-7751", "current_qty": 1, "threshold_qty": 5 }
]

docs.title: Add error handling
docs.text:
import fabric.functions as fn
import json
from datetime import datetime, timezone

udf = fn.UserDataFunctions()

@udf.connection(argName="businessEventsClient", alias="RetailInventory")
@udf.function()
def batch_publish(
    businessEventsClient: fn.FabricBusinessEventsClient,
    items_json: str
) -> str:
    try:
        items = json.loads(items_json)
    except (ValueError, TypeError):
        return "Invalid JSON input"

    if not isinstance(items, list) or len(items) == 0:
        return "Input must be a non-empty array"

    event_data = [
        {
            "store_id": item["store_id"],
            "product_id": item["product_id"],
            "current_qty": item["current_qty"],
            "threshold_qty": item["threshold_qty"],
            "occurred_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()
        }
        for item in items
    ]

    businessEventsClient.PublishEvent(
        type="Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold",
        event_data=event_data,
        data_version="v1"
    )

    return f"Published {len(event_data)} events"

docs.title: Considerations
docs.text:
Each item in the array becomes an independent event. The platform delivers each one individually, with its own retry window.

Validate array size before publishing. Very large arrays may hit request size limits. Filter the input to only include items that actually need an event.

docs.title: Chain Two Business Events
docs.text: Use the output of one Business Event as the trigger for publishing a second Business Event. This creates a lightweight event chain where each step signals the next.

docs.title: When to use this recipe
docs.text: Use event chaining when a business process has sequential stages and each stage has independent consumers. Chaining keeps each stage loosely coupled — the first publisher does not need to know what happens next.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    P1[Publisher\nNotebook] -->|Publishes| E1[Business Event A\nOrder.Processing.Completed]
    E1 --> ACT[Activator\nMonitors Event A]
    ACT -->|Condition met| P2[Activator publishes]
    P2 -->|Publishes| E2[Business Event B\nOrder.Fulfillment.Started]
    E2 --> C1[Eventhouse\nFulfillment analytics]
    E2 --> C2[Activator\nNotify warehouse]

docs.title: Step 1: Publish the first event
docs.text:
# Notebook publishes Event A when order processing completes
event_data = {
    "order_id": "ORD-4421",
    "customer_id": "CUST-882",
    "total_amount": 340.00,
    "completed_at": "2024-11-15T14:32:00Z"
}

notebookutils.businessEvents.publish(
    "MyWorkspace",
    "OrderProcessing",
    "Order.Processing.Completed",
    event_data,
    dataVersion="v1"
)

docs.title: Step 2: Configure Activator to publish Event B
docs.text:
1. Go to Real-Time Hub → Business events
  2. Find Order.Processing.Completed and click Set alert
  3. Configure Monitor: source = Order.Processing.Completed
  4. Configure Condition: On each event
  5. Configure Action: Publish a business event
  6. Select Order.Fulfillment.Started as the target event
  7. Map fields from Event A to Event B:
Event A field Event B field order_id order_id customer_id customer_id (static value) started_at → current timestamp

docs.title: Design considerations
docs.text:
Keep chains short. Each hop adds latency and a potential failure point. If you need more than 2-3 steps, consider whether an orchestration tool (Data Pipeline, Power Automate) is a better fit.

Each event should be independently meaningful. If Event B is only ever triggered by Event A and has no other consumers, evaluate whether two separate events are necessary.

Do not create circular chains. Event A triggering Event B triggering Event A will cause an infinite loop. Design chains to always move forward in the process.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text: Each scenario is a complete, end-to-end walkthrough of a real business problem solved with Business Events. Every scenario includes a business context, an architecture diagram, an Avro event schema, publisher code or UI setup, and consumer configuration.

docs.title: Detect & Alert
docs.text:
Use this pattern when you want to notify a person or system the moment a condition is met. The publisher detects a condition and emits an event. Activator evaluates a rule and immediately notifies a team or triggers a response. Eventhouse independently stores the same published findings for historical analysis, so these scenarios pair an immediate response with a queryable history.

Scenario Industry Publisher Consumer(s) Level Sales Volume Alert Retail Notebook Activator, Eventhouse Beginner Real-Time Stream Alert Finance Eventstream Activator, Eventhouse Intermediate Revenue Below Target Sales Activator Activator, Eventhouse Intermediate

Good first scenario

Start with Sales Volume Alert if you are new to Business Events. It covers the full publish-subscribe cycle with the minimum number of moving parts.

docs.title: Decide & Act
docs.text:
Use this pattern when you want one event to trigger multiple automated actions across independent systems. The publisher evaluates context — customer history, fraud rules, inventory levels, SLA data — makes a decision, and publishes an event that carries the outcome. Multiple independent consumers act on it simultaneously without knowing about each other. Adding a new action means adding a new subscription, not changing the publisher.

Scenario Industry Publisher Consumer(s) Level Customer Loyalty Milestone Retail Activator Activator, Eventhouse Intermediate Abandoned Cart Recovery Ecommerce User Data Function Activator, Eventhouse Intermediate Discount Approval Evaluation and Event Publication Sales User Data Function Activator, Eventstream, Eventhouse Intermediate Fraud Response Before Fulfillment Finance User Data Function Activator, Eventhouse Advanced Real-Time Viewer Recommendations Media User Data Function Activator, Eventhouse Advanced Shipment Delay Auto-Mitigation Logistics User Data Function Activator, Eventhouse Advanced

The fan-out advantage

Fraud Response Before Fulfillment and Shipment Delay Auto-Mitigation each trigger three independent Activator rules from a single event. This is the fan-out pattern: one publisher, many independent consumers, zero coordination overhead.

docs.title: Track & Analyze
docs.text:
Use this pattern when you want published events stored as queryable records. With Analyze in Eventhouse enabled during Business Event creation, received events are automatically persisted in a dedicated KQL table. These scenarios use that history for operational dashboards, audit trails, or replenishment planning without custom ingestion code. Low Stock Threshold also includes an Activator notification; Data Lineage Audit focuses on analytical history.

Scenario Industry Publisher Consumer(s) Level Low Stock Threshold Supply Chain User Data Function Activator, Eventhouse Beginner Data Lineage Audit DataOps Notebook Eventhouse Intermediate

Combine patterns

Sales Volume Alert, Real-Time Stream Alert, Customer Loyalty Milestone, Revenue Below Target, Low Stock Threshold, and Discount Approval Evaluation and Event Publication all pair Activator responses with Eventhouse history. The same combination appears in Abandoned Cart Recovery, Fraud Response Before Fulfillment, Real-Time Viewer Recommendations, and Shipment Delay Auto-Mitigation. Each walkthrough verifies both paths: the immediate response and the stored event.

docs.title: How to read a scenario
docs.text:
Each scenario follows the same structure:

  1. Business context — the real-world problem and why it matters
  2. Architecture — Mermaid flow diagram of the full solution
  3. Step 1: Create the Business Event — Avro schema definition
  4. Step 2: Publish from the source workload — publisher code (Notebook, User Data Function, Eventstream, or Activator)
  5. Step 3: Configure the consumer — Activator rule setup and/or KQL queries for Eventhouse
  6. Step 4: Test end to end — how to verify the full flow
  7. What happens next — extension ideas and related scenarios

docs.title: Abandoned Cart Recovery
docs.text: Publisher: User Data Function | Consumer: Activator, Eventhouse

docs.title: Business context
docs.text:
An ecommerce company already detects abandoned carts in its storefront and uses recovery campaigns to encourage customers to complete checkout. Marketing needs to act while an offer is still relevant, and analytics needs to measure which responses lead to purchases.

A User Data Function receives a webhook when the storefront identifies an abandoned cart. It retrieves the customer profile, evaluates offer eligibility, and publishes an Ecommerce.Cart.Abandoned Business Event. Activator initiates the recovery response, and Eventhouse stores received events for conversion analytics.

The problem without Business Events: Recovery can use existing campaigns and integrations. The scaling challenge is sharing the same abandonment and eligibility context with email, CRM, and analytics without embedding each channel's behavior in the function.

The solution with Business Events: The function publishes one event contract for the detected abandonment. Separate Activator rules handle the offer and CRM follow-up. Another channel can reuse that context without changing the publisher, provided it does not require additional fields or a different eligibility decision.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph External
        EC[Ecommerce\nStorefront]
    end

    subgraph Fabric
        UDF[User Data Function\nCart abandonment handler]
        FA[(Fabric Data + AI\nCustomer profile, cart history,\noffer rules)]
        BE([Business Event\n'Ecommerce.Cart.Abandoned'])
    end

    subgraph Consumers
        ACT1{Activator\nOffer rule}
        ACT2{Activator\nCRM rule}
        EH[(Eventhouse\nConversion analytics)]
    end

    EC -->|Cart webhook| UDF
    FA -.->|context| UDF
    UDF -->|Publish event| BE
    BE --> ACT1
    BE --> ACT2
    BE --> EH
    ACT1 --> EMAIL[Personalized\nrecovery email]
    ACT2 --> CRM[CRM\nfollow-up task]

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Business Event
docs.text:
Before publishing any event, define it in Real-Time Hub. Enable Eventhouse integration during this step.

  1. Go to Real-Time Hub → Business Events → Create.
  2. Create or select an Event Schema Set. Use EcommerceCart as the schema set name. You will need this name when connecting the Event Schema Set to the User Data Function through the connection manager.
  3. Name the event Ecommerce.Cart.Abandoned.

  4. In the schema editor, paste the following JSON:

    {
  "type": "record",
  "name": "Ecommerce.Cart.Abandoned",
  "fields": [
    {
      "name": "customer_id",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "Unique identifier of the customer"
    },
    {
      "name": "customer_email",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "Customer email address for recovery communication"
    },
    {
      "name": "cart_id",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "Unique identifier of the abandoned cart"
    },
    {
      "name": "cart_value",
      "type": "float",
      "doc": "Total value of items in the cart at time of abandonment"
    },
    {
      "name": "item_count",
      "type": "int",
      "doc": "Number of distinct items in the cart"
    },
    {
      "name": "last_activity_at",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "ISO 8601 timestamp of the last customer cart interaction"
    }
  ]
}

  5. Confirm that Analyze in Eventhouse is enabled. Create a new Eventhouse or select an existing one in your workspace. This creates a dedicated KQL table named Ecommerce.Cart.Abandoned automatically.

  6. Select Create.

docs.title: Step 2: Publisher - User Data Function
docs.text: The User Data Function receives a webhook from the ecommerce storefront and publishes the Business Event.

docs.title: Create the User Data Function
docs.text:
1. In your Fabric workspace, select + New item and create a User Data Function named PublishCartAbandonedEvent.
  2. Inside the UDF item, select New function.

docs.title: Connect to the schema set
docs.text:
1. In the Home ribbon, select Manage connections.
  2. Select + Add connection, search for EcommerceCart, and select Connect.
  3. Note the alias (EcommerceCart by default). Close the pane.

docs.title: Function code
docs.text:
import fabric.functions as fn
import logging

udf = fn.UserDataFunctions()

@udf.connection(argName='businessEventsClient', alias='EcommerceCart')
@udf.function()
def publish_cart_abandoned_event(
    businessEventsClient: fn.FabricBusinessEventsClient,
    customer_id: str,
    customer_email: str,
    cart_id: str,
    cart_value: float,
    item_count: int,
    last_activity_at: str
) -> str:
    logging.info("publish_cart_abandoned_event invoked.")

    event_data = {
        'customer_id': customer_id,
        'customer_email': customer_email,
        'cart_id': cart_id,
        'cart_value': cart_value,
        'item_count': item_count,
        'last_activity_at': last_activity_at,
    }

    businessEventsClient.PublishEvent(
        type='Ecommerce.Cart.Abandoned',
        event_data=event_data,
        data_version='v1'
    )

    return "Event 'Ecommerce.Cart.Abandoned' published successfully"

For full details on publishing Business Events from User Data Functions, see the User Data Function publisher documentation.

docs.title: Consumer 1 - Activator: Personalized recovery offer
docs.text:
1. In Real-Time Hub, locate Ecommerce.Cart.Abandoned under your schema set.
  2. Select Set alert and name the rule Cart Recovery - Offer.
  3. In the Monitor section, set Source to Business events and connect to Ecommerce.Cart.Abandoned.
  4. Set Condition to On each event. Add an optional filter on cart_value > 30 to focus recovery spend on higher-value carts.
  5. In the Action section, configure the email or Power Automate flow that sends the personalized recovery offer. Add customer_email, cart_id, and cart_value as context fields.
  6. Select Save.

docs.title: Consumer 2 - Activator: CRM follow-up task
docs.text:
1. In Real-Time Hub, locate Ecommerce.Cart.Abandoned.
  2. Select Set alert and name the rule Cart Recovery - CRM.
  3. Set Condition to On each event.
  4. In the Action section, configure the Power Automate flow that creates a CRM follow-up task. Add customer_id and cart_id as context fields.
  5. Select Save.

docs.title: Consumer 3 - Eventhouse: Conversion analytics
docs.text:
Eventhouse integration was enabled during event creation. Every published event is ingested into the Ecommerce.Cart.Abandoned KQL table automatically.

Open your Eventhouse KQL database and run the following queries to explore recovery patterns.

Peak abandonment windows — last 7 days:

['Ecommerce.Cart.Abandoned']
| where ingestion_time() > ago(7d)
| extend HourOfDay = hourofday(ingestion_time())
| summarize Abandonments = count() by HourOfDay
| order by Abandonments desc

High-value carts abandoned in the last 24 hours:

['Ecommerce.Cart.Abandoned']
| where ingestion_time() > ago(24h)
| where cart_value > 100
| project customer_id, cart_id, cart_value, item_count, last_activity_at
| order by cart_value desc

Daily abandonment volume trend:

['Ecommerce.Cart.Abandoned']
| where ingestion_time() > ago(30d)
| summarize Abandonments = count() by bin(ingestion_time(), 1d)
| order by ingestion_time() asc

docs.text:
Invoke publish_cart_abandoned_event with the following test values:

Parameter Value customer_id cust-5521 customer_email test@example.com cart_id cart-9987 cart_value 145.50 item_count 3 last_activity_at 2024-06-22T09:00:00Z

Then confirm the event arrived in Eventhouse:

['Ecommerce.Cart.Abandoned']
| where cart_id == "cart-9987"
| order by ingestion_time() desc
| take 1

If the row is present and the Activator offer rule fires, your end-to-end setup is working.

docs.title: Customer Loyalty Milestone
docs.text: Publisher: Activator | Consumers: Activator, Eventhouse

docs.title: Business context
docs.text:
A retail company already tracks cumulative customer spending across stores. When a customer reaches a loyalty milestone, such as $5,000 in spend, marketing needs to issue a reward, analytics needs to record the occurrence, and the CRM needs the new loyalty tier.

Each team owns a different system and response. They need a consistent definition of the milestone without having to reproduce the spending threshold in every application or coordinate every downstream update through the detection rule. Analytics also needs a queryable milestone history to compare tier activity across stores and look up a customer's milestone context.

The problem without Business Events: A shared rule or existing integrations can deliver the first implementation. If detection and all responses are maintained together, adding a team or changing a response requires coordination with the owner of that implementation. Separate detection rules can instead drift in their interpretation of the milestone.

The solution with Business Events: Activator keeps detecting the milestone and publishes a Retail.Customer.MilestoneReached event. Marketing and CRM responses use independent Activator rules, and Eventhouse records received events for analytics. Teams can add responses using the existing contract without changing detection; changes to the milestone definition still require agreement.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph Eventhouse source
        KQL[KQL Query\nCumulative spend\nper customer]
    end

    subgraph Activator Publisher
        RULE1{Condition:\ntotal_spend > threshold}
    end

    subgraph Real-Time Hub
        BE([Business Event\n'Retail.Customer.MilestoneReached'])
    end

    subgraph Consumers
        PA[Activator → Power Automate\nReward notification]
        EH[(Eventhouse\nMilestone history)]
        ANALYTICS[KQL analysis\nTier activity and customer history]
        CRM[Activator → Power Automate\nCRM tier update]
    end

    KQL -->|Monitor| RULE1
    RULE1 -->|Publish event| BE
    BE --> PA
    BE -->|Auto-ingest| EH
    BE --> CRM
    EH --> ANALYTICS
Component Role Source Eventhouse transactions table supplies customer spend; it is not the milestone-history table Publisher Activator detects the spend threshold crossing and publishes a milestone Consumer 1 Independent Activator rules invoke marketing and CRM Power Automate flows Consumer 2 Eventhouse stores the published milestones for analytics Schema set RetailCustomers Event type and KQL table Retail.Customer.MilestoneReached

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Business Event
docs.text:
Before configuring Activator, define the Business Event in Real-Time Hub.

  1. Go to Real-Time Hub → Business Events → Create.
  2. Create or select an Event Schema Set. Use RetailCustomers as the schema set name.
  3. Name the event Retail.Customer.MilestoneReached.

  4. In the schema editor, paste the following JSON:

    {
  "type": "record",
  "name": "Retail.Customer.MilestoneReached",
  "fields": [
    {
      "name": "customer_id",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "Unique identifier of the customer"
    },
    {
      "name": "customer_name",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "Full name of the customer"
    },
    {
      "name": "milestone_tier",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "Loyalty tier reached: silver, gold, or platinum"
    },
    {
      "name": "total_spend",
      "type": "float",
      "doc": "Cumulative spend amount that triggered this milestone"
    },
    {
      "name": "store_id",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "Identifier of the store where the milestone was reached"
    },
    {
      "name": "detected_at",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "Timestamp when the milestone was detected, ISO 8601 format"
    }
  ]
}

  5. Keep Analyze in Eventhouse enabled. Create a new Eventhouse or select an existing one in your workspace. Fabric automatically creates the dedicated Retail.Customer.MilestoneReached KQL table. This output table is separate from the transactions source table.

  6. Select Create.

docs.title: Step 2: Publisher - Activator
docs.text: Activator monitors a KQL query that computes cumulative customer spend. When the condition is met, it publishes the Business Event. There is no code to write.

docs.title: Create the Activator rule
docs.text:
1. In your Fabric workspace, open your KQL Queryset that queries the customer transaction table in your Eventhouse.

  2. Write or select a query that returns cumulative spend per customer, for example:

    transactions
| summarize total_spend = sum(amount) by customer_id, customer_name, store_id

  3. Select Set alert from the KQL Queryset toolbar.

  4. In the Activator rule pane, configure the condition:
    • Monitor: select the query result field total_spend
    • Condition: Becomes greater than
    • Value: 5000

Keep below-threshold customers in the query results so the publisher rule can observe a transition from at or below 5000 to above it. This sample evaluates spend per customer and store and maps the crossing to the gold tier.

docs.title: Configure the publish action
docs.text:
1. In the Action section, select Publish a business event.
  2. For Business event, select Retail.Customer.MilestoneReached.

  3. Map each schema field to the corresponding query result column or a static value:

    Schema field Source customer_id customer_id column customer_name customer_name column milestone_tier Static value: gold total_spend total_spend column store_id store_id column detected_at Dynamic: current timestamp

  4. Select Save to activate the rule.

For full details on using Activator as a Business Events publisher, see the Activator publisher documentation.

docs.title: Step 3: Consumer 1 - Marketing reward (Activator → Power Automate)
docs.text:
1. In Real-Time Hub, locate Retail.Customer.MilestoneReached under your schema set.
  2. Select Set alert.
  3. Name the rule Loyalty Milestone - Reward.
  4. In the Monitor section, set Source to Business events and connect to Retail.Customer.MilestoneReached.
  5. Set Condition to On each event.
  6. In the Action section, select Power Automate and connect the flow that sends the reward notification.
  7. Add customer_id, customer_name, and milestone_tier as context fields.
  8. Select Save.

docs.title: Step 4: Consumer 2 - Analytics (Eventhouse)
docs.text:
The Eventhouse consumer was enabled in Step 1. It receives the published milestone independently of the marketing and CRM rules. No separate ingestion configuration or custom table name is needed.

Open the selected Eventhouse KQL database and query the automatically created Retail.Customer.MilestoneReached table. Use bracket syntax because the table name preserves dots.

Inspect the latest milestone events:

['Retail.Customer.MilestoneReached']
| order by ingestion_time() desc
| take 50

Compare milestone activity by store and tier:

['Retail.Customer.MilestoneReached']
| where ingestion_time() > ago(30d)
| summarize ReceivedMilestones = count(),
    Customers = dcount(customer_id) by store_id, milestone_tier
| order by ReceivedMilestones desc

Look up a test customer's milestone history:

['Retail.Customer.MilestoneReached']
| where customer_id == "cust-loyalty-demo-001"
| project DetectedAt = todatetime(detected_at), ReceivedAt = ingestion_time(),
    customer_id, milestone_tier, total_spend, store_id
| order by DetectedAt desc

This table records milestone signals, not every purchase, successful reward delivery, or completed CRM updates. Repeated publications or deliveries can increase event counts. Measuring reward redemption or CRM completion requires outcomes from those systems.

Use the tier-activity query in a Real-Time Dashboard for marketing and store operations. See Eventhouse and Business Events integration for dashboard setup.

docs.title: Step 5: Consumer 3 - CRM tier update (Activator → Power Automate)
docs.text:
Repeat the same steps as Consumer 1 with a different Power Automate flow:

  1. In Real-Time Hub, locate Retail.Customer.MilestoneReached.
  2. Select Set alert.
  3. Name the rule Loyalty Milestone - CRM Update.
  4. Set Condition to On each event.
  5. Connect the Power Automate flow that updates the customer's loyalty tier in the CRM.
  6. Add customer_id and milestone_tier as context fields.
  7. Select Save.

docs.title: Step 6: End-to-end test
docs.text:
Use synthetic customer transactions in your test workspace to produce a real threshold crossing. Running the KQL query alone does not publish an event; the saved Activator publisher rule must evaluate the changed result.

  1. Prepare source transactions for a new test customer, for example cust-loyalty-demo-001 at store-mx-042, totaling 4900. Keep customer_name consistent between records. Use a new customer ID for each test run.
  2. Let the Activator publisher evaluate the below-threshold result. Confirm that no milestone is published for this test customer yet.
  3. Add a 200 transaction for that customer and store through your test data source. The query now returns 5100.
  4. Let the publisher evaluate the changed result. In Real-Time Hub, open Retail.Customer.MilestoneReached, confirm that the publisher rule is listed on the Publisher tab, and verify the customer ID, gold tier, and 5100 spend in Data preview.
  5. Confirm that the marketing Power Automate flow runs and sends the reward notification.
  6. Run the customer-history query from Step 4. Confirm that the Eventhouse table contains the same customer ID, tier, spend, and store as the published event.
  7. Confirm separately that the CRM Power Automate flow runs and updates the tier.

The test is complete only when both Activator response flows and the Eventhouse history are verified. A row in the history table proves analytical delivery of the milestone; it does not prove that either Power Automate flow completed.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Each team controls its own consumer. Marketing can update the reward flow without involving analytics or CRM. Analytics can change queries and dashboards over the milestone-history table without touching the detection rule. A customer success team can add a Teams notification through another Activator rule using the same contract. The Eventhouse source query remains responsible for spend calculations; the separate history table records the milestones the publisher emits.

docs.title: Data Lineage Audit
docs.text: Publisher: Notebook | Consumer: Eventhouse

docs.title: Business context
docs.text:
A data engineering team runs a series of daily notebooks in Microsoft Fabric that ingest, transform, and load data across multiple domains. Each run must be auditable: when it ran, what it processed, whether it succeeded or failed, and who or what triggered it.

The notebooks already produce operational logs. The team also needs a consistent run-completion record across domains so it can compare outcomes and investigate recurring failures without interpreting a different log format for each notebook.

The problem without Business Events: A shared logging library or audit table can already centralize these records. The challenge is maintaining a common run-completion contract as more notebooks and consumers participate, rather than coupling each notebook to every reporting destination.

The solution with Business Events: Each notebook publishes a DataOps.Pipeline.RunCompleted event using the same schema. With Eventhouse integration enabled, received events form a queryable record of reported runs. This complements operational logs; it does not by itself provide complete lineage or establish compliance.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Fabric Notebooks
        NB1[Ingestion\nNotebook]
        NB2[Transformation\nNotebook]
        NB3[Load\nNotebook]
    end

    subgraph Real-Time Hub
        BE([Business Event\n'DataOps.Pipeline.RunCompleted'])
    end

    subgraph Eventhouse
        EH[(Audit\nKQL Database)]
    end

    NB1 -->|Publish event| BE
    NB2 -->|Publish event| BE
    NB3 -->|Publish event| BE
    BE -->|Auto-ingest| EH

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Business Event
docs.text:
Before publishing any event, define it in Real-Time Hub. Eventhouse integration is enabled by default during this step.

  1. Go to Real-Time Hub → Business Events → Create.
  2. Create or select an Event Schema Set. Use DataOps as the schema set name. Note the name and workspace. They map directly to SCHEMA_SET_NAME and WORKSPACE_NAME in the publisher code.
  3. Name the event DataOps.Pipeline.RunCompleted.

  4. In the schema editor, paste the following JSON:

    {
  "type": "record",
  "name": "DataOps.Pipeline.RunCompleted",
  "fields": [
    {
      "name": "pipeline_id",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "Unique identifier of the pipeline or notebook"
    },
    {
      "name": "pipeline_name",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "Human-readable name of the pipeline or notebook"
    },
    {
      "name": "run_id",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "Unique identifier of this specific run"
    },
    {
      "name": "status",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "Outcome of the run: completed, failed, or skipped"
    },
    {
      "name": "rows_processed",
      "type": "int",
      "doc": "Number of rows processed during this run"
    },
    {
      "name": "duration_seconds",
      "type": "int",
      "doc": "Total execution time in seconds"
    },
    {
      "name": "triggered_by",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "What triggered the run: schedule, manual, or upstream"
    },
    {
      "name": "completed_at",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "Timestamp when the run completed, ISO 8601 format"
    }
  ]
}

  5. Confirm that Analyze in Eventhouse is enabled. Create a new Eventhouse or select an existing one in your workspace. This creates a dedicated KQL table for this Business Event automatically.

  6. Select Create.

docs.title: Step 2: Publisher - Notebook
docs.text: Add the following code at the end of each notebook you want to audit. The event is published after the notebook completes its main logic, capturing the actual outcome.

docs.title: Create the Notebook
docs.text:
1. Open the notebook you want to instrument, or create a new one in your Fabric workspace.
  2. Add a new cell at the end of the notebook for the audit event.

docs.title: Notebook code
docs.text:
Replace WORKSPACE_NAME and SCHEMA_SET_NAME with the values from Step 1. Replace the hardcoded values with variables from your notebook's actual execution context.

# Publish a DataOps.Pipeline.RunCompleted Business Event from a Fabric Notebook
# notebookutils reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/fabric/data-engineering/microsoft-spark-utilities

import uuid
from datetime import datetime, timezone

WORKSPACE_NAME = "<your-workspace-name>"
SCHEMA_SET_NAME = 'DataOps'
EVENT_NAME = 'DataOps.Pipeline.RunCompleted'

# Replace with actual values from your notebook execution context
payload = {
    'pipeline_id': "nb-ingestion-sales-daily",
    'pipeline_name': "Sales Daily Ingestion",
    'run_id': str(uuid.uuid4()),
    'status': 'completed',
    'rows_processed': 48320,
    'duration_seconds': 142,
    'triggered_by': 'schedule',
    'completed_at': datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()
}

# Publish to Business Events
notebookutils.businessEvents.publish(
    eventSchemaSetWorkspace=WORKSPACE_NAME,
    eventSchemaSet=SCHEMA_SET_NAME,
    eventTypeName=EVENT_NAME,
    eventData=payload,
    dataVersion='v1'
)

docs.title: Step 3: Consumer - Eventhouse
docs.text:
Because Eventhouse integration was enabled during Business Event creation, a dedicated KQL table was created automatically. Every run across all instrumented notebooks is ingested into that table with no additional configuration.

Open your Eventhouse KQL database and run the following queries to explore the audit data.

View the most recent pipeline runs:

['DataOps.Pipeline.RunCompleted']
| order by ingestion_time() desc
| take 50

Count failures per pipeline over the last 30 days:

['DataOps.Pipeline.RunCompleted']
| where ingestion_time() > ago(30d)
| where status == 'failed'
| summarize FailureCount = count() by pipeline_name
| order by FailureCount desc

Track average run duration per pipeline:

['DataOps.Pipeline.RunCompleted']
| where ingestion_time() > ago(7d)
| summarize AvgDuration = avg(duration_seconds), RunCount = count() by pipeline_name
| order by AvgDuration desc

Audit trail for a specific pipeline:

['DataOps.Pipeline.RunCompleted']
| where pipeline_id == "nb-ingestion-sales-daily"
| project completed_at, status, rows_processed, duration_seconds, triggered_by
| order by completed_at desc

For more information, see Eventhouse and Business Events integration.

docs.title: Step 4: End-to-end test
docs.text:
Once you have the Business Event defined, the notebook instrumented, and the Eventhouse integration active, run the notebook once. Then verify the audit record in Eventhouse:

['DataOps.Pipeline.RunCompleted']
| where pipeline_id == "nb-ingestion-sales-daily"
| order by ingestion_time() desc
| take 1

If the row is present with the correct run_id and completed_at, your audit pipeline is working. You can then add the publish cell to all notebooks you want to track.

docs.text:

    EH --> RTD[Real-Time Dashboard\npipeline health view]
    EH --> ACT[Activator rule\nfailure alert]

docs.title: Discount Approval Evaluation and Event Publication
docs.text: Publisher: User Data Function | Consumers: Activator, Eventstream, Eventhouse

docs.title: Business context
docs.text:
A sales team already applies commercial policy when negotiating deals. A proposed discount or estimated margin can require manager or executive review. Sellers need an immediate evaluation result, while approval operations and analytics need a consistent representation of the review requirement.

The problem without Business Events: Policy evaluation can already live in a shared service. The scaling challenge is keeping that evaluation separate from each approval, notification, and analytics integration, so new consumers do not require the sales application to reproduce policy or manage another downstream call.

The solution with Business Events: The sales application sends proposal facts to a Fabric User Data Function. The UDF owns policy evaluation, returns the approval level synchronously, and publishes Sales.Deals.DiscountApprovalRequired only for manager or executive review. Activator notifies approval operations, while Eventstream and Eventhouse consume the same contract independently for downstream processing and analytics. The event communicates that review is required; it does not mean approval has been granted.

This public sample reuses the demonstrated FabCon code path: a browser application, a server-side Python proxy, Azure CLI delegated authentication for development, and the tested UDF request and response contract. This walkthrough adds a separately configured Activator notification without changing that executable contract. See the sample README.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph Sales application
        APP[Commercial review page]
        PROXY[Python server-side proxy]
        APP -->|Proposal facts| PROXY
    end

    subgraph Fabric
        UDF["User Data Function<br/>Evaluate discount policy"]
        BE(["Business Event<br/>Discount approval required"])
        ES[Eventstream]
        EH[(Eventhouse)]
        ACT[Activator]
        TEAMS[Teams notification\nApproval operations]
    end

    PROXY -->|Authenticated request| UDF
    UDF -.->|Synchronous result| PROXY
    UDF -->|Manager or executive review| BE
    BE --> ES
    BE --> EH
    BE --> ACT
    ACT --> TEAMS

The dashed arrow is the synchronous evaluation response. The event path is asynchronous. The proxy uses an Azure CLI delegated token and maps snake_case proposal facts to camelCase UDF parameters.

Component Name Responsibility Sales application Commercial review page Collects proposal facts and displays the synchronous result Server-side adapter Python proxy Validates input, acquires a development token, maps fields, and invokes the UDF Publisher and policy owner DiscountApprovalPublisher Evaluates commercial policy and conditionally calls PublishEvent Event Schema Set CommercialGovernance Holds the governed v1 event definition Business Event Sales.Deals.DiscountApprovalRequired Signals that manager or executive review is required Eventstream DiscountApprovalStream Receives approval-required events for downstream processing Eventhouse DiscountApprovalAnalytics Stores approval-required events for analytics Activator Discount Review Required Sends approval operations the proposal and required review level

The command and event paths have different success conditions. A successful UDF response can report that publication was requested. It does not prove that an event reached publisher preview, Eventstream, Eventhouse, or another consumer. Verify delivery separately.

docs.title: Policy paths
docs.text:
Path Condition Synchronous result Business Event Within policy Discount is at most 10% and margin is at least 25% approval_level: none Not published Manager approval Discount is greater than 10% and at most 15%, and margin is at least 25% approval_level: manager Publication requested Executive approval Discount is greater than 15% or margin is below 25% approval_level: executive Publication requested

The executive rule takes precedence. A 12% discount with a 24% margin requires executive approval.

docs.title: Create and connect the User Data Function
docs.text:
1. In the Fabric workspace, create a User Data Function named DiscountApprovalPublisher.
  2. Open the UDF item.
  3. In Home, select Manage connections.
  4. Select Add connection.
  5. Search for CommercialGovernance and select it.
  6. Copy the generated alias into the @udf.connection decorator.
  7. Copy the complete sample from evaluate_discount_request.py into the UDF editor.

The executable sample preserves the demonstrated policy rules, event type, nine payload fields, data_version="v1", and return fields:

return {
    "approval_level": approval_level,
    "event_published": True,
    "message": (
        f"Deal {dealId} requires {approval_level} approval. "
        "Business Event published."
    ),
}

It adds public-sample validation without changing the policy or payload contract:

  • Non-empty string and length validation for dealId, accountName, and region
  • Finite and range validation for deal value, discount, and margin
  • Time-zone-aware UTC validation for eventTime

docs.title: Connect the sales application
docs.text:
The companion sample contains the browser app and Python proxy.

The browser sends the demonstrated snake_case request:

{
  "deal_id": "DEAL-2048",
  "account_name": "Sample Health",
  "region": "West",
  "deal_value": 450000.0,
  "requested_discount_percent": 18.0,
  "estimated_margin_percent": 22.0,
  "event_time": "2026-09-15T17:15:00Z"
}

The proxy maps it explicitly to the exact UDF parameters:

Application field UDF parameter deal_id dealId account_name accountName region region deal_value dealValue requested_discount_percent requestedDiscountPercent estimated_margin_percent estimatedMarginPercent event_time eventTime

Publish the UDF, enable its public URL, and grant the developer Execute permission. Then authenticate with Azure CLI and start the sample:

az login
python server.py --mode fabric --udf-url "<public UDF URL>"

The public UDF URL is supplied only at startup. It is not stored in browser code or committed. The proxy acquires a delegated development token server-side for:

https://analysis.windows.net/powerbi/api/user_impersonation

Azure CLI delegated authentication is the demonstrated developer path. It is not a production identity design. Production hosting must use an approved, configurable identity and token lifecycle. Tokens must never be logged or exposed to the browser.

The proxy uses the demonstrated 120-second timeout by default. Use --timeout to configure it. If token acquisition or Fabric invocation fails, the proxy returns a clear error and does not fall back to local simulation.

docs.title: Parse the Fabric response
docs.text:
The proxy applies the empirically supported response behavior:

  • status must equal Succeeded.
  • errors supplies failure details.
  • output can be a JSON object or a JSON string.
  • approval_level, event_published, and message are required.
  • Additional envelope and output fields are tolerated.
  • invocationId is optional and is preserved as invocation_id when present.

The application normalizes event_published to publication_requested. This label is intentionally narrower. A true value means PublishEvent returned during UDF execution. It does not confirm downstream delivery.

For explicit fallback testing only:

python server.py --mode local

Local simulation applies the same policy but never calls Fabric and always reports publication_requested: false.

docs.text:
1. Open Sales.Deals.DiscountApprovalRequired in Real-Time Hub.
  2. Select Add consumer, then Eventstream.
  3. Select the target workspace.
  4. Name the Eventstream DiscountApprovalStream.
  5. Review the configuration and select Connect.
  6. Open the Eventstream and use Data preview to confirm approval-required events arrive.

docs.text:
Because Analyze in Eventhouse was enabled, Fabric creates the KQL table automatically.

['Sales.Deals.DiscountApprovalRequired']
| where ingestion_time() > ago(24h)
| project
    event_time,
    deal_id,
    account_name,
    region,
    deal_value,
    requested_discount_percent,
    estimated_margin_percent,
    approval_level,
    approval_reason

These rows represent published exceptions only. They cannot calculate the share of all proposals that were within policy unless another governed dataset records the full proposal population.

docs.title: Consumer 3: Activator notification
docs.text:
1. In Real-Time Hub, locate Sales.Deals.DiscountApprovalRequired under CommercialGovernance.
  2. Select Set alert and name the rule Discount Review Required.
  3. In Monitor, select Business events and connect to that event.
  4. Set Condition to On each event. The UDF has already evaluated the discount and margin policy.
  5. In Action, select Teams, then Channel post, and choose the approval operations channel.
  6. Include deal_id, approval_level, approval_reason, and region as context. Use the existing proposal system to look up additional details rather than posting unnecessary customer data.
  7. Save the rule.

This consumer notifies the team that review is required. It does not assign an approver or capture an approval decision. Eventhouse ingestion and Eventstream delivery do not depend on the notification completing.

docs.title: Step 4: End-to-end test
docs.text:
Run the automated sample tests:

python -m unittest -v

The tests cover exact field mapping, policy boundaries, validation, Fabric status and errors, object and string outputs, optional diagnostics, 120-second and configured timeouts, Azure CLI failures, no automatic fallback, and local plus mocked Fabric HTTP paths. Automated tests do not require a real endpoint.

For an optional live call, use the sanitized verify_live.py:

python verify_live.py --udf-url "<public UDF URL>"

The script invokes the configured UDF and checks the synchronous executive result. It does not automate a browser or recording workflow.

After a live manager or executive evaluation:

  1. Confirm the application shows the expected approval_level and publication_requested: true.
  2. In the Business Event's publisher preview, verify the matching deal_id.
  3. In DiscountApprovalStream Data preview, verify the same event separately.
  4. Query DiscountApprovalAnalytics and confirm the event fields.
  5. Confirm that the Teams notification contains the same deal_id, required approval_level, and approval_reason.
  6. Confirm within-policy requests are absent from event consumers and produce no Teams review notification.

The walkthrough is complete only when the synchronous evaluation, Eventstream receipt, Eventhouse row, and Activator notification have each been verified. A successful UDF response alone does not establish downstream delivery.

docs.title: What happens next
docs.text:
The executable sample stops at evaluation and event publication request. This walkthrough also configures analytics and a review-required notification. It does not implement:

  • Approver assignment
  • Approve or reject capture
  • SLA timers, reminders, or escalation
  • CRM or sales application updates
  • Final decision correlation

Extend the notification with an approval workflow and a separate versioned decision contract for those responsibilities. If revision-safe correlation is required, introduce evaluation_id in schema v2 and design consumers for idempotency.

Treat account_name as customer data. Prefer a pseudonymous identifier when the display name is unnecessary, restrict Eventhouse and Eventstream access to approved roles, and retain the field only for the documented purpose and minimum required period.

For more detail, use the sample README, UDF publisher documentation, Eventstream overview, schema versioning guidance, and retry guidance.

docs.title: Fraud Response Before Fulfillment
docs.text: Publisher: User Data Function | Consumer: Activator, Eventhouse

docs.title: Business context
docs.text:
An ecommerce marketplace already evaluates order risk using customer history, payment metadata, and fraud rules. It needs to hold or review high-risk orders before fulfillment while allowing legitimate purchases to proceed.

A User Data Function receives an order webhook, evaluates the risk score against customer history, payment metadata, and fraud rules stored in Fabric, and publishes two Business Events: Ecommerce.Order.HighRiskDetected captures the signal, and Ecommerce.Order.FraudDecision carries the decision outcome (hold, manual review, or release). Three independent Activator rules act on the decision. Eventhouse stores the full audit trail for compliance and pattern analysis.

The problem without Business Events: Risk evaluation can already run in a function or application. If each downstream system receives a separate integration or reproduces the decision logic, changes become harder to coordinate and teams may act on different interpretations of the same assessment.

The solution with Business Events: The function publishes separate contracts for the detected risk and the resulting decision. Activator rules use the decision event for hold, review, or release actions, while Eventhouse supports analysis of received events. New consumers can reuse these contracts; changes to risk policy still belong in the evaluator.
