docs.text: The User Data Function evaluates each order, makes a risk decision, and publishes both Business Events.

docs.title: Create the User Data Function
docs.text:
1. In your Fabric workspace, select + New item and create a User Data Function named EvaluateHighRiskOrder.
  2. Inside the UDF item, select New function.

docs.title: Connect to the schema set
docs.text:
1. In the Home ribbon, select Manage connections.
  2. Select + Add connection, search for EcommerceOrders, and select Connect.
  3. Note the alias (EcommerceOrders by default). Close the pane.

docs.title: Function code
docs.text:
import fabric.functions as fn
from datetime import datetime, timezone
import logging

udf = fn.UserDataFunctions()

@udf.connection(argName='businessEventsClient', alias='EcommerceOrders')
@udf.function()
def evaluate_high_risk_order(
    businessEventsClient: fn.FabricBusinessEventsClient,
    order_id: str,
    customer_id: str,
    risk_score: float,
    amount: float,
    payment_method: str
) -> str:
    logging.info("evaluate_high_risk_order invoked.")

    detected_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()

    # Publish the signal event — consumers can react to the raw detection
    businessEventsClient.PublishEvent(
        type='Ecommerce.Order.HighRiskDetected',
        event_data={
            'order_id': order_id,
            'customer_id': customer_id,
            'risk_score': risk_score,
            'amount': amount,
            'payment_method': payment_method,
            'detected_at': detected_at,
        },
        data_version='v1'
    )

    # Decision logic — thresholds can be loaded from Lakehouse or SQL DB
    if risk_score >= 0.85:
        decision = 'hold'
    elif risk_score >= 0.55:
        decision = 'manual_review'
    else:
        decision = 'release'

    # Publish the decision event — downstream consumers act on this independently
    businessEventsClient.PublishEvent(
        type='Ecommerce.Order.FraudDecision',
        event_data={
            'order_id': order_id,
            'customer_id': customer_id,
            'risk_score': risk_score,
            'decision': decision,
            'decided_at': datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
        },
        data_version='v1'
    )

    return f"Order {order_id}: decision = {decision}"

For full details on publishing Business Events from User Data Functions, see the User Data Function publisher documentation.

docs.title: Low Stock Threshold
docs.text: Publisher: User Data Function | Consumers: Activator, Eventhouse

docs.title: Business context
docs.text:
A retail company already uses an external warehouse management system (WMS) to track stock and detect when a product falls below its reorder threshold. The inventory team needs a consistent record of these occurrences to identify recurring shortages and inform replenishment decisions.

The WMS sends a webhook to a User Data Function in Microsoft Fabric. The function normalizes the payload and publishes a Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold Business Event. Activator notifies inventory planning immediately, while Eventhouse retains the same finding for KQL analysis of recurring shortages across products and stores.

The problem without Business Events: The WMS can continue detecting low stock, and existing integrations can continue responding. The sharing challenge is agreeing on one low-stock contract rather than creating a different payload and integration for each new consumer.

The solution with Business Events: The User Data Function publishes the detected condition using a shared schema. Activator sends a Teams notification with the product and stock context, and Eventhouse independently stores received events for analysis. Neither consumer replaces WMS detection or requires a separate call from the function. The alert informs replenishment planning; it does not place an order.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph External
        WMS[Warehouse\nManagement System]
    end

    subgraph Fabric
        UDF[User Data Function\nWebhook receiver]
        BE([Business Event\n'Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold'])
        EH[(Eventhouse\nKQL Database)]
        ACT[Activator\nOn each event]
        TEAMS[Teams notification\nInventory planning]
    end

    WMS -->|HTTP webhook| UDF
    UDF -->|Publish event| BE
    BE -->|Auto-ingest| EH
    BE --> ACT
    ACT --> TEAMS
Component Role Publisher User Data Function normalizes the WMS low-stock finding Consumer 1 Activator sends a Teams notification to inventory planning Consumer 2 Eventhouse stores the finding for shortage analysis Schema set RetailInventory Event type and KQL table Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Business Event
docs.text:
Before publishing any event, define it in Real-Time Hub. Eventhouse integration is enabled by default during this step.

  1. Go to Real-Time Hub → Business Events → Create.
  2. Create or select an Event Schema Set. Use RetailInventory as the schema set name. You will need this name later when connecting the Event Schema Set to the User Data Function through the connection manager.
  3. Name the event Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold.

  4. In the schema editor, paste the following JSON:

    {
  "type": "record",
  "name": "Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold",
  "fields": [
    {
      "name": "product_id",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "Unique identifier of the product"
    },
    {
      "name": "product_name",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "Display name of the product"
    },
    {
      "name": "store_id",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "Identifier of the store or warehouse reporting the condition"
    },
    {
      "name": "current_stock",
      "type": "int",
      "doc": "Current units available at the time of detection"
    },
    {
      "name": "threshold",
      "type": "int",
      "doc": "Minimum stock level that triggered this alert"
    },
    {
      "name": "supplier_id",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "Identifier of the preferred supplier for reordering"
    },
    {
      "name": "detected_at",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "Timestamp when the condition was detected, ISO 8601 format"
    }
  ]
}

  5. Confirm that Analyze in Eventhouse is enabled. Create a new Eventhouse or select an existing one in your workspace. This creates a dedicated KQL table for this Business Event automatically. No additional ingestion configuration is needed.

  6. Select Create.

docs.title: Step 2: Publisher - User Data Function
docs.text: The User Data Function receives a webhook from the external WMS and publishes the Business Event.

docs.title: Create the User Data Function
docs.text:
1. In your Fabric workspace, select + New item and create a User Data Function named PublishLowStockEvent.
  2. Inside the UDF item, select New function.

docs.title: Connect to the schema set
docs.text:
Before writing the code, you need to connect the function to the Event Schema Set.

  1. In the Home ribbon, select Manage connections.
  2. In the Connections pane, select + Add connection.
  3. Search for RetailInventory, select the schema set, and select Connect.
  4. An alias is automatically generated using the schema set name (RetailInventory by default). Add this alias to the @udf.connection decorator in your function code.
  5. Close the Manage connections pane.

docs.title: Function code
docs.text:
Replace the default function code with the following. For full details on publishing Business Events from User Data Functions, see the User Data Function publisher documentation and the end-to-end tutorial.

import fabric.functions as fn
import logging

udf = fn.UserDataFunctions()

# The alias must match the connection configured in Manage connections
@udf.connection(argName='businessEventsClient', alias='RetailInventory')
@udf.function()
def publish_low_stock_event(
    businessEventsClient: fn.FabricBusinessEventsClient,
    product_id: str,
    product_name: str,
    store_id: str,
    current_stock: int,
    threshold: int,
    supplier_id: str,
    detected_at: str
) -> str:
    logging.info("publish_low_stock_event invoked.")

    event_data = {
        'product_id': product_id,
        'product_name': product_name,
        'store_id': store_id,
        'current_stock': current_stock,
        'threshold': threshold,
        'supplier_id': supplier_id,
        'detected_at': detected_at
    }

    businessEventsClient.PublishEvent(
        type='Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold',
        event_data=event_data,
        data_version='v1'
    )

    return "Event 'Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold' published successfully"

docs.title: Consumer 1: Notify inventory planning with Activator
docs.text:
1. In Real-Time Hub, locate Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold under RetailInventory.
  2. Select Set alert and name the rule Low Stock - Inventory Planning.
  3. In Monitor, select Business events and connect to Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold.
  4. Set Condition to On each event. The WMS has already detected the low-stock condition; this rule does not reproduce that detector.
  5. In Action, select Teams, then Channel post, and choose the inventory planning channel.
  6. Include product_id, store_id, current_stock, threshold, and supplier_id in the context.
  7. Save the rule.

docs.title: Consumer 2: Analyze shortages in Eventhouse
docs.text:
Because Eventhouse integration was enabled during Business Event creation, a dedicated KQL table was created automatically in your Eventhouse database. Every published event is ingested into that table with no additional configuration.

Open your Eventhouse KQL database and run the following queries to verify events are flowing and explore the data.

View the most recent events:

['Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold']
| order by ingestion_time() desc
| take 50

Count alerts per store over the last 7 days:

['Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold']
| where ingestion_time() > ago(7d)
| summarize AlertCount = count() by store_id
| order by AlertCount desc

Identify products with recurring low stock:

['Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold']
| where ingestion_time() > ago(30d)
| summarize Occurrences = count(), AvgStock = avg(current_stock) by product_id, product_name
| where Occurrences > 3
| order by Occurrences desc

For more information, see Eventhouse and Business Events integration.

docs.title: Step 4: End-to-end test
docs.text:
Once you have the Business Event defined, the User Data Function connected, and the Eventhouse integration active, invoke the function with hardcoded values to verify the full flow.

Call publish_low_stock_event with the following test values:

Parameter Value product_id prod-mx-7821 product_name Wireless Keyboard store_id store-mx-042 current_stock 4 threshold 10 supplier_id sup-451 detected_at 2024-06-22T09:00:00Z

Then run the following KQL query in your Eventhouse database and confirm the row appears:

['Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold']
| where product_id == "prod-mx-7821"
| order by ingestion_time() desc
| take 1

Also confirm that the Teams notification contains prod-mx-7821, store-mx-042, current stock 4, and threshold 10. The test is complete only when both the notification and the Eventhouse row are verified. The row does not confirm that an order was placed or stock was replenished.

You can then configure the external WMS to call the User Data Function endpoint as a webhook.

docs.title: What happens next
docs.text:
With immediate notifications in Activator and history in Eventhouse, the inventory team can extend either response without modifying the publisher.

    BE([Business Event\n'Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold']) --> EH[(Eventhouse)]
    BE --> ACT[Activator]
    ACT --> TEAMS[Teams notification]
    EH --> KQL[KQL queries\nand analysis]
    EH --> RTD[Real-Time Dashboard\nlive operational view]
    EH --> ML[ML model input\npredictive reorder]
Extension What it enables Real-Time Dashboard Live tile showing current low-stock alerts across all stores KQL scheduled query Daily summary of products below threshold sent to a report ML model input Historical event data as training features for reorder prediction Additional Activator rule Add a separately configured replenishment workflow without changing the User Data Function

For full details on querying and visualizing Business Events in Eventhouse, see the Eventhouse integration documentation.

docs.title: Real-Time Stream Alert
docs.text: Publisher: Eventstream | Consumers: Activator, Eventhouse

docs.title: Business context
docs.text:
A retail company processes a continuous stream of payment transactions from multiple stores and channels. Most transactions are routine, but high-value transactions above a defined threshold require immediate review by the fraud team.

Eventstream already evaluates the transaction stream and can identify records above the threshold. This scenario publishes that finding as a Retail.Payment.HighValueTransaction Business Event. The fraud team needs an immediate notification, while payment operations needs a history of selected transactions to compare high-value activity by store, payment method, and currency. A high value indicates a review condition, not proof of fraud.

The problem without Business Events: A direct Activator rule on the stream may be sufficient for one alert. When more teams need the high-value signal, separate filters and integrations can duplicate its definition and make threshold changes harder to coordinate.

The solution with Business Events: Eventstream keeps the filter and publishes the matching transaction through a named contract. Activator uses that event for the review notification, and Eventhouse independently stores the same event for historical analysis. Adding analytics does not require another high-value filter, a separate Eventstream-to-Eventhouse destination, or alert-channel logic in the publisher.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph Sources
        PS[Payment\nTransaction Stream]
    end

    subgraph Fabric
        ES[Eventstream\namount > 5000]
        BE([Business Event\n'Retail.Payment.HighValueTransaction'])
        ACT{Activator\nRule}
        TEAMS[Teams alert\nFraud review team]
        EH[(Eventhouse\nHigh-value transaction history)]
        KQL[KQL analysis\nStore, payment method and currency]
    end

    PS -->|Continuous stream| ES
    ES -->|Filter match| BE
    BE -->|Trigger| ACT
    ACT --> TEAMS
    BE -->|Auto-ingest| EH
    EH --> KQL
Component Role Publisher Eventstream filters payment records where amount > 5000 Consumer 1 Activator sends a Teams notification for each received high-value event Consumer 2 Eventhouse stores the selected payment events for historical analysis Schema set RetailPayments Event type and KQL table Retail.Payment.HighValueTransaction

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Business Event
docs.text:
Before configuring the Eventstream, define the Business Event in Real-Time Hub.

  1. Go to Real-Time Hub → Business Events → Create.
  2. Create or select an Event Schema Set. Use RetailPayments as the schema set name.
  3. Name the event Retail.Payment.HighValueTransaction.

  4. In the schema editor, paste the following JSON:

    },
    {
      "name": "payment_method",

      "doc": "Payment method used: credit_card, debit_card, or digital_wallet"
    },
    {
      "name": "amount",
      "type": "float",
      "doc": "Transaction amount in the store's local currency"
    },
    {

docs.text: Eventstream is configured entirely from the UI. There is no code to write. You apply a filter transformation to the transaction stream and route matching events to the Business Event destination.

docs.title: Create the Eventstream
docs.text:
1. In your Fabric workspace, select + New item and create an Eventstream named PaymentTransactionStream.
  2. In the Eventstream editor, add your payment transaction data source. Connect it to the stream that produces transaction records with at least the fields defined in the schema above.

docs.text:
1. On the Transform events or add destination card, select the down arrow and choose Filter.
  2. Select the Action link on the Filter card.
  3. In the Filter window, configure the following:
    • Operation name: HighValueFilter
    • Field: amount
    • Condition: Greater than
    • Value: 5000
  4. Select Save.

docs.title: Add the Business Events destination
docs.text:
1. On the HighValueFilter card, select Action or the + button.
  2. In the list of destinations, select Business events.
  3. On the Business events card, select the Edit (pencil icon).
  4. In the Business events window:
    • For Destination name, enter HighValueTransactionPublisher.
    • For Business event type, select Choose and select Retail.Payment.HighValueTransaction.

docs.text:
1. On the Retail.Payment.HighValueTransaction card, select Add next to Add a mapper to map schema.
  2. In the Map schema window, verify that each stream field maps to the corresponding schema field, and select Finish.
  3. Select Publish to activate the Eventstream.

For full details on configuring Eventstream as a Business Events publisher, see the Eventstream publisher documentation and the end-to-end tutorial.

docs.title: Consumer 1: Notify reviewers with Activator
docs.text: When a Retail.Payment.HighValueTransaction event is published, Activator evaluates the rule and triggers a Teams alert to the fraud review team.

docs.title: Set up the alert rule
docs.text:
1. In Microsoft Fabric, navigate to Real-Time on the left navigation bar.
  2. Select Business events in Real-Time Hub.
  3. Locate the Retail.Payment.HighValueTransaction event under your schema set.
  4. Select Set alert from the event options.

docs.title: Configure the rule
docs.text:
Details section

Enter a name for the rule, for example: High Value Transaction Alert.

Monitor section

  1. In the Source field, select Business events.
  2. In the Connect data source wizard, select the Retail.Payment.HighValueTransaction event type.
  3. Select Next, review the settings, and select Save.

Condition section

Set Check to On each event.

Action section

  1. For Select action, choose Teams then Channel post.
  2. Configure the Teams channel for the fraud review team.
  3. In Context, add transaction_id, amount, store_id, and payment_method so the alert includes the relevant details.
  4. Save and activate the rule.

docs.title: Consumer 2: Analyze high-value activity in Eventhouse
docs.text:
Open the Eventhouse KQL database selected in Step 1. Its dedicated table receives the Business Events independently of Activator and Teams. It contains the high-value findings published by Eventstream, not the full raw payment stream or the outcome of a fraud review.

Inspect the latest high-value events:

['Retail.Payment.HighValueTransaction']
| order by ingestion_time() desc
| take 50

Compare received high-value activity by store and payment method:

['Retail.Payment.HighValueTransaction']
| where ingestion_time() > ago(7d)
| summarize ReceivedEvents = count(), LargestAmount = max(amount)
    by store_id, payment_method, currency
| order by ReceivedEvents desc

Track hourly high-value event volume by currency:

['Retail.Payment.HighValueTransaction']
| where ingestion_time() > ago(24h)
| summarize ReceivedEvents = count()
    by currency, ReceivedHour = bin(ingestion_time(), 1h)
| order by ReceivedHour asc

Amounts are in the transaction's local currency. Keep currency in monetary comparisons rather than adding unlike currencies. The sample threshold is 5000 local-currency units; currency-specific thresholds are a separate policy decision. Counts represent received event records and can include repeated publications or deliveries. Calculating the high-value share of all payments requires the underlying payment stream as well.

Save these queries to a Real-Time Dashboard for payment operations. See Eventhouse and Business Events integration for the dashboard steps.

docs.title: Step 4: End-to-end test
docs.text:
With the Eventstream published, the Activator rule saved, and Eventhouse integration enabled, send these two records through the configured payment source. Use new transaction IDs for each test run.

Field Above-threshold record Boundary record transaction_id demo-review-6001 demo-boundary-5000 payment_method credit_card credit_card amount 6000 5000 currency MXN MXN store_id store-mx-042 store-mx-042 processed_at Current UTC time in ISO 8601 format Current UTC time in ISO 8601 format
  1. In Real-Time Hub, select Retail.Payment.HighValueTransaction and confirm that PaymentTransactionStream appears on the Publisher tab.
  2. On the Data preview tab, select that publisher and confirm that the 6000 record appears. The 5000 record should not be published because the filter is strictly greater than 5000.
  3. Confirm that the Teams notification contains the above-threshold transaction's ID and amount. The boundary record should not trigger this rule.

  4. In the Eventhouse KQL database, run:

    ['Retail.Payment.HighValueTransaction']
| where ingestion_time() > ago(1h)
| where transaction_id in ("demo-review-6001", "demo-boundary-5000")
| project ReceivedAt = ingestion_time(), transaction_id, amount,
    currency, store_id, payment_method
| order by ReceivedAt desc

  5. Confirm that the above-threshold transaction is stored and that the boundary transaction is absent from this Business Event table.

The test is complete only when the matching payment reaches both the Teams notification and Eventhouse, and the boundary payment reaches neither. The raw source may still retain both payments. An Eventhouse row verifies analytical delivery, not completion of a fraud review or a payment block.

docs.title: What happens next
docs.text:
The same high-value finding now supports immediate review and historical payment analysis. Further consumers can be added without changing the Eventstream filter. Review decisions, case status, and confirmed fraud outcomes must be captured separately if analytics needs those outcomes.

docs.title: Real-Time Viewer Recommendations
docs.text: Publisher: User Data Function | Consumer: Activator, Eventhouse

docs.title: Business context
docs.text:
A streaming platform already uses viewer profiles, interaction history, and a recommendation model to personalize content. It wants recent interactions to inform recommendations during the current session, while analytics measures engagement and model performance.

A User Data Function receives a webhook for a selected viewer interaction: a click, a search, a skip, or a sustained watch. It retrieves profile and interaction context from Fabric, calls the recommendation model, and publishes a Streaming.Viewer.BehaviorDetected Business Event. Activator triggers a recommendation refresh, and Eventhouse stores received events for click-through rate analysis and model retraining.

The problem without Business Events: The platform can already refresh recommendations through application integrations. As experimentation and analytics teams need the same finding, adding a separate call or interpretation for each consumer makes the function harder to evolve.

The solution with Business Events: The function shares the selected interaction and recommendation context through one event contract. Activator handles the refresh response, while analytics queries received events in Eventhouse. Consumers that use the existing contract can be added without changing the function; Business Events do not replace the recommendation model or raw interaction ingestion.

  4. In Action, configure the User Data Function or Power Automate flow that calls the recommendation serving layer to refresh the viewer's queue. Add viewer_id, session_id, and content_id as context fields.

docs.title: Consumer 2 - Eventhouse: Viewer telemetry
docs.text:
Eventhouse integration was enabled during event creation. Every published event is ingested into the Streaming.Viewer.BehaviorDetected KQL table automatically.

Recommendation refresh rate — events per hour, last 24 hours:

['Streaming.Viewer.BehaviorDetected']
| where ingestion_time() > ago(24h)
| summarize EventCount = count() by bin(ingestion_time(), 1h)
| order by ingestion_time() asc

Most engaged content by interaction type:

| where action in ('watch', 'like')
| summarize Engagements = count() by content_id, action

Viewer session activity — depth of interaction:

| summarize

docs.title: Step 4: End-to-end test
docs.text:
Invoke publish_viewer_behavior_event with the following test values:

Parameter Value viewer_id viewer-7712 session_id sess-3301 content_id content-882 action watch occurred_at 2024-06-22T09:00:00Z

Then confirm the event arrived in Eventhouse:

['Streaming.Viewer.BehaviorDetected']
| where viewer_id == "viewer-7712"
| order by ingestion_time() desc
| take 1

If the row is present and the Activator refresh rule fires, your end-to-end setup is working.

With behavior events flowing, analytics and personalization teams can build independently on the same signal.

docs.title: Revenue Below Target
docs.text: Publisher: Activator | Consumers: Activator, Eventhouse

docs.title: Business context
docs.text:
A sales team tracks revenue against regional targets in a Power BI report. When revenue falls more than 15% below the target for the same reporting period, the business owner needs a notification and refreshed investigation data. Sales operations also needs a history of the detected shortfalls to compare patterns across regions and periods.

The problem without Business Events: A direct alert can notify the first owner. If each downstream workflow also calculates the variance, the threshold definition and reporting context can drift between teams. Adding historical analysis should not require another detector.

The solution with Business Events: An Activator publisher monitors the report's revenue-variance measure and publishes Sales.Revenue.BelowTarget when the variance crosses below -15%. Independent Activator consumer rules notify the owner and run an investigation-data pipeline. Eventhouse stores the same signal for historical analysis. A stored shortfall is not proof that the owner responded or that revenue recovered.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    PBI[Power BI report\nRevenue and target by region]
    PUB{Activator publisher\nVariance becomes less than -15%}
    BE([Business Event\n'Sales.Revenue.BelowTarget'])
    ALERT[Activator consumer\nTeams notification]
    PIPE[Activator consumer\nInvestigation data pipeline]
    EH[(Eventhouse\nShortfall history)]
    KQL[KQL analysis\nRegion and reporting period]

    PBI --> PUB
    PUB -->|Publish finding| BE
    BE --> ALERT
    BE --> PIPE
    BE -->|Auto-ingest| EH
    EH --> KQL
Component Role Source Power BI report backed by a semantic model with revenue and targets for the same period and currency Publisher Activator detects a variance crossing below -15% Consumer 1 Independent Activator rules notify the owner and run an investigation-data pipeline Consumer 2 Eventhouse stores received shortfall signals for analysis Schema set SalesPerformance Event type and KQL table Sales.Revenue.BelowTarget

Before starting, prepare a test report and a Data Factory pipeline that refreshes investigation data. The pipeline is a consumer action, not the source of the report's threshold calculation.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Business Event
docs.text:
1. Go to Real-Time Hub, Business Events, Create.
  2. Create or select an Event Schema Set named SalesPerformance.
  3. Name the event Sales.Revenue.BelowTarget.

  4. In the schema editor, paste:

    {
  "type": "record",
  "name": "Sales.Revenue.BelowTarget",
  "fields": [
    {
      "name": "region",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "Sales region whose revenue is below target"
    },
    {
      "name": "period_start",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "Start of the reporting period in ISO 8601 format"
    },
    {
      "name": "revenue",
      "type": "double",
      "doc": "Revenue for the reporting period in the report's currency"
    },
    {
      "name": "target",
      "type": "double",
      "doc": "Positive revenue target for the same reporting period and currency"
    },
    {
      "name": "variance_pct",
      "type": "double",
      "doc": "100 * (revenue - target) / target; negative values mean below target"
    },
    {
      "name": "detected_at",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "Time the publisher detected the shortfall, ISO 8601 UTC format"
    }
  ]
}

  5. Keep Analyze in Eventhouse enabled. Create a new Eventhouse or select an existing one in your workspace. Fabric automatically creates the dedicated Sales.Revenue.BelowTarget KQL table.

  6. Select Create.

docs.title: Step 2: Publisher - Activator on a Power BI report
Prepare the report
docs.text:
Use a test semantic model with a RevenuePerformance table containing region, period_start, revenue, and target. Keep one reporting period and currency in the test report's filter context. Start with one region, for example West, revenue 90000, and target 100000.

Create a numeric measure for percentage variance:

variance_pct =
VAR RevenueAmount = SUM(RevenuePerformance[revenue])
VAR TargetAmount = SUM(RevenuePerformance[target])
RETURN
    IF(
        TargetAmount > 0,
        100 * DIVIDE(RevenueAmount - TargetAmount, TargetAmount)
    )

This measure returns -10 for the starting values, not -0.10. Do not apply percentage formatting that multiplies it by 100 again. Zero or negative targets do not produce a valid variance in this example.

Create a supported report visual for revenue variance by region. Include the revenue, target, region, and period context needed for parameter mapping. The report's data refresh and the Activator evaluation cadence determine when a change is detected; publishing does not make the semantic model update continuously.

docs.title: Configure the publisher
docs.text:
1. On the report visual, select Set alert, then Open in Activator.
  2. Monitor variance_pct and set the condition to Becomes less than, with value -15.
  3. In Action, select Publish a business event.
  4. Select Sales.Revenue.BelowTarget.

  5. Map the fields:

    Schema field Source region Region from the monitored visual period_start Reporting period from the visual, or a static ISO 8601 value for the single-period test revenue Revenue for the monitored region and period target Target for the same region and period variance_pct The numeric variance measure detected_at Dynamic current UTC timestamp

  6. Save and activate the publisher rule.

For production data, supply the current period dynamically rather than leaving a static test value. See Activator as a Business Events publisher for report entry points and field mapping.

docs.title: Consumer 1: Notify the business owner
docs.text:
1. In Real-Time Hub, locate Sales.Revenue.BelowTarget under SalesPerformance.
  2. Select Set alert and name the rule Revenue Shortfall - Owner Notification.
  3. In Monitor, select Business events and connect to this event.
  4. Set Condition to On each event. The publisher already owns the shortfall threshold.
  5. In Action, select Teams, then Channel post, and choose the test sales-operations channel.
  6. Include region, period_start, revenue, target, and variance_pct in the context.
  7. Save the consumer rule.

For multiple regional owners, configure the destination or region-specific consumer rules according to your ownership model.

docs.title: Consumer 2: Refresh investigation data
docs.text:
Create a second Activator consumer rule on the same Business Event, again using On each event. Name it Revenue Shortfall - Investigation Data, select the Data Pipeline action, and choose the prepared investigation-data pipeline. Configure any parameters required by that pipeline and save the rule.

Keep this consumer separate from the publisher and notification rule. Do not have the investigation pipeline modify the source report's revenue or target values as part of this test.

docs.title: Consumer 3: Analyze shortfalls in Eventhouse
docs.text:
Open the Eventhouse KQL database selected in Step 1. No separate ingestion configuration is needed.

Inspect recent shortfalls:

['Sales.Revenue.BelowTarget']
| order by ingestion_time() desc
| take 50

Compare received findings by region and reporting period:

['Sales.Revenue.BelowTarget']
| where ingestion_time() > ago(30d)
| summarize ReceivedFindings = count(), WorstVariancePct = min(variance_pct)
    by region, period_start
| order by ReceivedFindings desc, WorstVariancePct asc

These are counts of received shortfall records, not unique incidents or lost revenue. Repeated publications or deliveries can increase counts. The table contains only published shortfalls, so measuring overall target attainment also requires the source revenue and target data.

Save the comparison query to a Real-Time Dashboard for sales operations. See Eventhouse and Business Events integration.

docs.title: Step 4: End-to-end test
docs.text:
Use the test region and reporting period from Step 2. Allow the report to refresh and the Activator publisher to evaluate after each change.

  1. With revenue 90000 and target 100000, confirm a variance of -10. Let the publisher observe this initial state.
  2. Change revenue to 85000, refresh the report, and let the publisher evaluate. A variance of exactly -15 should not publish an event because the condition is strictly less than -15.
  3. Change revenue to 80000, refresh the report, and let the publisher evaluate. Confirm the -20 shortfall in the Business Event's publisher data preview.
  4. Verify the Teams notification contains the same region, period, and variance.
  5. Verify the investigation-data pipeline run completes in its run history.

  6. In the Eventhouse database, run:

    ['Sales.Revenue.BelowTarget']
| where ingestion_time() > ago(1h)
| where region == "West"
| project ReceivedAt = ingestion_time(), region, period_start,
    revenue, target, variance_pct
| order by ReceivedAt desc

  7. Confirm a row for revenue 80000, target 100000, and variance -20. The boundary value -15 should not appear as a newly published shortfall from this test.

The test is complete only when the notification, pipeline run, and Eventhouse row are verified independently. Use a fresh region or isolate the test period when repeating the test so earlier findings are not mistaken for new ones.

docs.title: What happens next
docs.text: Add regional response rules or analytics tiles using the same contract without changing the report's detector. Capture owner acknowledgement and investigation outcomes separately if you need to measure response effectiveness. The Business Event communicates a detected shortfall, not recovery or case completion.

docs.title: Sales Volume Alert
docs.text: Publisher: Notebook | Consumers: Activator, Eventhouse

docs.title: Business context
docs.text:
A retail company runs daily sales processing in Microsoft Fabric. Each store is expected to process a baseline number of transactions per hour based on historical data. If a store's transaction volume drops significantly below its expected baseline, it may indicate a failure in the point-of-sale integration, not a natural slowdown.

The notebook already compares actual volume with the baseline. Operations needs that finding in time to investigate a possible integration failure. Retail analytics needs a history of the same findings to identify stores with recurring volume drops and compare their severity over time.

The problem without Business Events: If the notebook calls each notification or analytics service directly, adding a response means updating the detection workload. Separate implementations can also interpret the same volume drop differently.

The solution with Business Events: The notebook keeps its detection logic and publishes a Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert event with the store and deviation context. Two independent consumers use that contract: Activator notifies operations for deviations below -30%, while Eventhouse retains every received finding for historical analysis, including findings that do not match the alert rule. The notebook does not call either consumer directly.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph Fabric Notebook
        A[Detect volume drop\nper store per hour]
    end

    subgraph Real-Time Hub
        B([Business Event\n'Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert'])
    end

    subgraph Activator
        C{Evaluate rule:\ndeviation_pct < -30}
        D[Send Teams alert\nto ops team]
    end

    subgraph Eventhouse
        E[(Volume alert history)]
        F[KQL analysis\nRecurring drops by store]
    end

    A -->|Publish event| B
    B -->|Trigger| C
    C -->|Threshold met| D
    B -->|Auto-ingest| E
    E --> F
Component Role Publisher Notebook calculates the volume deviation and publishes the finding Consumer 1 Activator filters for deviations below -30% and sends a Teams alert Consumer 2 Eventhouse stores received findings for recurrence and severity analysis Schema set RetailSales Event type and KQL table Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Business Event
docs.text:
Before publishing any event, you need to define it in Real-Time Hub.

  1. Go to Real-Time Hub → Business Events → Create.
  2. Create or select an Event Schema Set. Use RetailSales as the schema set name. Note the name and workspace. They map directly to SCHEMA_SET_NAME and WORKSPACE_NAME in the publisher code.
  3. Name the event Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert.

  4. In the schema editor, paste the following JSON:

    {
  "type": "record",
  "name": "Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert",
  "fields": [
    {
      "name": "store_id",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "Unique identifier of the store reporting the alert"
    },
    {
      "name": "expected_transactions",
      "type": "int",
      "doc": "Expected number of transactions based on historical average"
    },
    {
      "name": "actual_transactions",
      "type": "int",
      "doc": "Actual transactions recorded in the current monitoring window"
    },
    {
      "name": "deviation_pct",
      "type": "float",
      "doc": "Percentage deviation from expected volume. Negative means below expected."
    },
    {
      "name": "window_start",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "Start of the monitoring window in ISO 8601 format"
    },
    {
      "name": "severity",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "Alert severity level: low, medium, high"
    }
  ]
}

  5. Keep Analyze in Eventhouse enabled. Create a new Eventhouse or select an existing one in your workspace. Fabric automatically creates the dedicated Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert KQL table.

  6. Select Create. No separate ingestion pipeline or direct Notebook-to-Eventhouse write is needed.

docs.title: Step 2: Publisher - Notebook
docs.text: The notebook queries the sales data, calculates the deviation per store, and publishes a Business Event for each store that exceeds the threshold.

docs.title: Create the Notebook
docs.text:
1. In your Fabric workspace, select + New item and create a Notebook.
  2. Attach it to a Lakehouse that contains your sales data, or use the hardcoded values provided below for testing.

docs.title: Notebook code
docs.text:
Replace WORKSPACE_NAME with your Fabric workspace name and SCHEMA_SET_NAME with the name of the Event Schema Set associated with the Business Event you created in Real-Time Hub → Business Events.

# Publish a Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert Business Event from a Fabric Notebook
# notebookutils reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/fabric/data-engineering/microsoft-spark-utilities

WORKSPACE_NAME = "<your-workspace-name>"
SCHEMA_SET_NAME = "<your-schema-set-name>"
EVENT_NAME = 'Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert'

# Calculate deviation for a store
store_id = "store-mx-042"
expected = 1250
actual = 743
deviation_pct = round(((actual - expected) / expected) * 100, 2)
severity = 'high' if deviation_pct < -30 else 'medium' if deviation_pct < -15 else 'low'

# Build the event payload
payload = {
    'store_id': store_id,
    'expected_transactions': expected,
    'actual_transactions': actual,
    'deviation_pct': deviation_pct,
    'window_start': "2024-06-22T09:00:00Z",
    'severity': severity
}

# Publish to Business Events
notebookutils.businessEvents.publish(
    eventSchemaSetWorkspace=WORKSPACE_NAME,
    eventSchemaSet=SCHEMA_SET_NAME,
    eventTypeName=EVENT_NAME,
    eventData=payload,
    dataVersion='v1'
)

docs.title: Consumer 1: Notify operations with Activator
docs.text: When the Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert Business Event is published to Real-Time Hub, Activator can subscribe to it and trigger an action when the rule condition is met.

docs.title: Set up the alert rule
docs.text:
1. In Microsoft Fabric, navigate to Real-Time on the left navigation bar.
  2. Select Business events in Real-Time Hub.
  3. Locate the Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert event under your schema set.
  4. Select Set alert from the event options.

docs.title: Configure the rule
docs.text:
Details section

Enter a name for the rule, for example: Sales Volume Drop Alert.

Monitor section

  1. In the Source field, select Business events.
  2. In the Connect data source wizard, select the Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert event type.
  3. Select + Filter and configure the following filter:
    • Field: deviation_pct
    • Operator: Less than
    • Value: -30
  4. Select Next, review the settings, and select Save.

Condition section

Set Check to On each event.

Action section

  1. For Select action, choose Teams then Channel post.
  2. Configure the Teams channel to notify the operations team.
  3. In Context, add store_id, actual_transactions, and deviation_pct so the alert includes the relevant details.
  4. Save and activate the rule.

docs.title: Consumer 2: Analyze recurring drops in Eventhouse
docs.text:
Eventhouse integration was enabled in Step 1. Open the selected Eventhouse KQL database and query the automatically created table. The table name preserves dots, so use bracket syntax. Ingestion does not depend on the Activator filter or on Teams delivery.

Inspect the latest findings:

['Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert']
| order by ingestion_time() desc
| take 50

Find stores with repeated high-severity findings received in the last 7 days:

['Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert']
| where ingestion_time() > ago(7d)
| where deviation_pct < -30
| summarize HighSeverityFindings = count(),
    WorstDeviationPct = min(deviation_pct) by store_id
| order by HighSeverityFindings desc, WorstDeviationPct asc

Compare the severity mix of received findings over time:

['Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert']
| where ingestion_time() > ago(7d)
| summarize Findings = count() by severity, ReceivedHour = bin(ingestion_time(), 1h)
| order by ReceivedHour asc

These queries count received event records, not confirmed incidents or distinct monitoring windows. Repeated publications or deliveries can increase the counts. A volume drop still needs investigation; the history does not prove a point-of-sale failure.

Use the recurrence query as a tile in a Real-Time Dashboard for operations reviews. See Eventhouse and Business Events integration for querying and dashboard setup.

docs.title: Step 4: End-to-end test
docs.text:
Verify both consumers with two publications from the same notebook:

  1. Run the notebook as-is. The values for store-mx-042 produce a deviation_pct of -40.56 and severity of high.
  2. Confirm that the Teams alert includes the store and deviation.
  3. Change actual to 1000, leaving expected at 1250, and run the notebook again. This publishes a -20.0 deviation with medium severity. This event should be retained in Eventhouse but should not match the Activator filter.

  4. In the Eventhouse KQL database, run:

    ['Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert']
| where ingestion_time() > ago(1h)
| where store_id == "store-mx-042"
| project ReceivedAt = ingestion_time(), store_id,
    expected_transactions, actual_transactions, deviation_pct, severity
| order by ReceivedAt desc

  5. Confirm that records for both actual_transactions values, 743 and 1000, appear. Only the -40.56 finding should match the Teams alert rule.

The test is complete when the high-severity finding reaches Teams and both findings are queryable in Eventhouse. Data preview or a successful publish call alone does not verify both consumers. The queries filter on receipt time because the hardcoded window_start is a sample timestamp. Replace the sample values with real sales windows when connecting the notebook to production data.

docs.title: What happens next
docs.text:
The scenario now pairs an immediate response with a queryable history. Activator can add other actions, while analytics can build dashboards from the existing Eventhouse table. Neither extension requires adding consumer-specific logic to the notebook.

flowchart LR
    BE([Business Event\n'Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert']) -->|rule match| ACT[Activator]
    BE --> EH[(Eventhouse\nFinding history)]
    EH --> KQL[Recurrence and severity analysis]
    ACT --> TEAMS[Teams / Email alert]
    ACT --> PA[Power Automate flow]
    ACT --> NB[Notebook]
    ACT --> DP[Data Pipeline]
    ACT --> UDF[User Data Function]
Action When to use Teams / Email alert Notify a team or individual immediately when the condition is met Power Automate flow Trigger a business process or approval workflow outside Fabric Notebook Run a remediation or deeper analysis in response to the event Data Pipeline Kick off a downstream data processing job User Data Function Call custom logic or an external API

For full details on configuring each action type, see the Activator documentation.

docs.title: Shipment Delay Auto-Mitigation
docs.text: Publisher: User Data Function | Consumer: Activator, Eventhouse

docs.title: Business context
docs.text:
A logistics company already tracks shipments across carriers and routes. When its supply chain system detects a delay, operations needs to assess the affected order, available inventory, alternate routes, and customer commitments while there is still time to reduce the impact.

A User Data Function receives the delay signal, retrieves order, inventory, route, and SLA context from Fabric, calls an AI model to generate a mitigation plan, and publishes a Supply.Chain.ShipmentDelayed Business Event. Three independent Activator rules use the event for rerouting, inventory reallocation, and customer notification. Eventhouse records received events for SLA reporting and route performance analysis.

The problem without Business Events: Existing tracking and mitigation tools can handle individual delays. As more teams need the finding, embedding each response in the function couples delay interpretation to routing, inventory, notification, and audit integrations.

The solution with Business Events: The function shares the delay and mitigation context through one event contract. Each response is configured separately in Activator, so a new consumer can reuse the finding without changing detection. Coordinating potentially conflicting mitigation actions remains a responsibility of the consuming workflows.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph External["Source"]
        SC["Supply chain systems"]
    end

    subgraph Detection["Enrich the detected delay"]
        FA[("Fabric Data + AI<br/>Mitigation context")]
        UDF["User Data Function<br/>Delay mitigator"]
    end

    BE(["Business Event<br/>Shipment delayed"])

    ACT1{"Activator<br/>Reroute rule"}
    ACT2{"Activator<br/>Reallocate rule"}
    ACT3{"Activator<br/>Notify rule"}
    ROUTE["Reroute shipment"]
    INV["Reallocate inventory"]
    CUST["Notify customer"]

    EH[("Eventhouse<br/>SLA analytics")]

    SC -->|Delay webhook| UDF
    FA -->|Context + mitigation plan| UDF
    UDF -->|Publish event| BE
    BE --> ACT1
    BE --> ACT2
    BE --> ACT3
    BE --> EH
    ACT1 --> ROUTE
    ACT2 --> INV
    ACT3 --> CUST

Arrows show data flow. The event is published and consumed asynchronously; the three response branches are independent, not a prescribed sequence. Data and AI enrichment belong to the publisher, not the event-delivery path.

Component Contract or responsibility Fabric Data + AI Orders, inventory, routes, SLA rules, and the AI model used to generate a mitigation plan User Data Function Enriches the detected delay and publishes the event Shipment delayed Supply.Chain.ShipmentDelayed Activator rules Invoke separate rerouting, inventory reallocation, and customer notification workflows Eventhouse Stores received events for SLA reporting and route performance analysis

docs.text:
1. Go to Real-Time Hub → Business Events → Create.
  2. Create or select an Event Schema Set. Use SupplyChain as the schema set name. You will need this name when connecting the Event Schema Set to the User Data Function through the connection manager.
  3. Name the event Supply.Chain.ShipmentDelayed.

  4. In the schema editor, paste the following JSON:

    {
      "name": "shipment_id",

    },
    {

    },
    {

    },
    {

  6. Select Create.

docs.title: Step 2: Publisher - User Data Function
docs.text: The User Data Function receives a delay signal, enriches it with Fabric data and AI context, and publishes the Business Event.

docs.title: Create the User Data Function
docs.text:
1. In your Fabric workspace, select + New item and create a User Data Function named PublishShipmentDelayedEvent.
  2. Inside the UDF item, select New function.

docs.title: Connect to the schema set
docs.text:
1. In the Home ribbon, select Manage connections.
  2. Select + Add connection, search for SupplyChain, and select Connect.
  3. Note the alias (SupplyChain by default). Close the pane.

docs.title: Function code
docs.text:
import fabric.functions as fn
from datetime import datetime, timezone
import logging

udf = fn.UserDataFunctions()

@udf.connection(argName='businessEventsClient', alias='SupplyChain')
@udf.function()
def publish_shipment_delayed_event(
    businessEventsClient: fn.FabricBusinessEventsClient,
    shipment_id: str,
    order_id: str,
    route_id: str,
    carrier_id: str,
    delay_minutes: int,
    sla_breach: bool
) -> str:
    logging.info("publish_shipment_delayed_event invoked.")

    event_data = {
        'shipment_id': shipment_id,
        'order_id': order_id,
        'route_id': route_id,
        'carrier_id': carrier_id,
        'delay_minutes': delay_minutes,
        'sla_breach': sla_breach,
        'detected_at': datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
    }

    businessEventsClient.PublishEvent(
        type='Supply.Chain.ShipmentDelayed',
        event_data=event_data,
        data_version='v1'
    )

    return f"Event 'Supply.Chain.ShipmentDelayed' published for shipment {shipment_id}"

For full details on publishing Business Events from User Data Functions, see the User Data Function publisher documentation.

docs.title: Consumer 1 - Activator: Reroute shipment
docs.text:
1. In Real-Time Hub, locate Supply.Chain.ShipmentDelayed.
  2. Select Set alert and name the rule Delay - Reroute Shipment.
  3. Set Condition to On each event. Add filter: sla_breach == true.
  4. In Action, configure the Power Automate flow or webhook that calls the routing system to switch the shipment to an alternate route. Add shipment_id, route_id, and delay_minutes as context fields.
  5. Select Save.

docs.title: Consumer 2 - Activator: Reallocate inventory
docs.text:
1. Locate Supply.Chain.ShipmentDelayed and select Set alert.
  2. Name the rule Delay - Reallocate Inventory. Add filter: delay_minutes > 240.
  3. In Action, configure the flow that triggers an inventory reallocation from the nearest fulfillment center. Add order_id and shipment_id as context fields.
  4. Select Save.

docs.title: Consumer 3 - Activator: Notify customer
docs.text:
1. Locate Supply.Chain.ShipmentDelayed and select Set alert.
  2. Name the rule Delay - Notify Customer.
  3. Set Condition to On each event (notify for all delays, not only SLA breaches).
  4. In Action, configure the email or SMS notification flow. Add order_id, delay_minutes, and sla_breach as context fields.
  5. Select Save.

docs.title: Consumer 4 - Eventhouse: SLA analytics
docs.text:
Every delay event is ingested automatically. Use the following queries to monitor route performance and SLA impact.

Delays by route — last 7 days:

['Supply.Chain.ShipmentDelayed']
| where ingestion_time() > ago(7d)
| summarize DelayCount = count(), AvgDelay = avg(delay_minutes) by route_id
| order by DelayCount desc

SLA breach rate by carrier:

['Supply.Chain.ShipmentDelayed']
| where ingestion_time() > ago(30d)
| summarize
    Total = count(),
    Breaches = countif(sla_breach == true)
  by carrier_id
| extend BreachRate = round(todouble(Breaches) / Total * 100, 1)
| order by BreachRate desc

Delay trend over the last 30 days:

['Supply.Chain.ShipmentDelayed']
| where ingestion_time() > ago(30d)
| summarize
    Delays = count(),
    AvgDelayMins = avg(delay_minutes),
    SLABreaches = countif(sla_breach == true)
  by bin(ingestion_time(), 1d)
| order by ingestion_time() asc

docs.title: Step 4: End-to-end test
docs.text:
Invoke publish_shipment_delayed_event with the following test values:

Parameter Value shipment_id shp-77412 order_id ord-55200 route_id route-mx-la carrier_id carrier-004 delay_minutes 300 sla_breach true

Then confirm the event arrived in Eventhouse:

['Supply.Chain.ShipmentDelayed']
| where shipment_id == "shp-77412"
| project shipment_id, route_id, delay_minutes, sla_breach, detected_at
| take 1

If the row is present and all three Activator rules fire, your end-to-end setup is working.
